label: S. 140
title: Wildfire Prevention Act of 2026
one: Sets rising targets for forest thinning and prescribed burns on federal land, speeds up environmental review for some projects, adds data reporting, and also wipes out the 2001 Roadless Rule that protects about 58 million acres of national forest from road building.
summary:
This bill aims to cut wildfire risk on National Forest and Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land. It tells the agencies to work out how many acres they thinned and burned on purpose (prescribed fire) from 2021 to 2025. Starting in 2027 they must set yearly goals at least equal to that average. Goals rise to 20% above it in 2029 and 30 and 40% above it from 2031 on. The bill requires standard ways of tracking this work, public yearly reports, and budget reports that include cost per acre and whether the work reduced fire risk or helped land health.

It also makes several changes that speed up or ease logging and land use. Utility companies could cut trees up to 150 feet from power lines on federal land, up from 10 feet. The size limit for timber sales that can skip some formal bidding steps rises from $10,000 to $55,000. Removing dangerous trees near roads, trails and campgrounds, on up to 6,000 acres, would skip full environmental review. Agencies must use existing fast-track review tools. Local governments and tribes could step into lawsuits over nearby wildfire or timber projects. The agencies must study using livestock grazing to cut fuels. A seven-year pilot program would test wildfire technology from private firms, nonprofits and universities. A required report on wildfire costs (FLAME report) is repealed.

Finally, Title IV cancels the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule and bars the Forest Service from making a similar one. Idaho and Colorado state rules stay in place.
does: Requires yearly goals for mechanical thinning and prescribed fire on Forest Service and BLM land, rising to at least 40% above the 2021-2025 average by FY2031.
Requires state-by-state acreage allotments within 90 days of enactment, and exempts setting these goals from NEPA environmental review.
Requires standardized data tracking, public annual reports, and budget-linked reports covering cost per acre, wildfire risk, effectiveness and land-health benefits.

Raises the distance for hazard tree removal near power lines on federal land from 10 to 150 feet and lets utilities cut vegetation in rights-of-way without a separate timber sale; any sale proceeds go to the agency.
Changes the definition of 'owner or operator' of power facilities so it no longer includes contractors or agents.
Raises a National Forest timber sale threshold from $10,000 to $55,000.

Creates a categorical exclusion (skips full environmental review) for removing high-priority hazard trees near roads, trails and developed recreation sites, up to 6,000 acres, excluding wilderness and some other areas.
Gives local governments and tribes the right to intervene in lawsuits over nearby approved wildfire-risk or timber-revenue projects and join settlement talks.
Directs a strategy on using livestock grazing to cut wildfire fuels, including use of vacant allotments in drought or disaster.
Requires use of existing streamlined environmental review authorities on units with land at risk from insects, disease or high wildfire hazard.
Sets up a 7-year public-private wildfire technology testbed pilot program run by the Interior Department's Wildland Fire Service.
Repeals a FLAME Act reporting requirement.
Nullifies the 2001 Roadless Rule and bars similar future rules, while keeping the Idaho and Colorado state rules.
who: Residents and communities near national forests and BLM land, especially in the wildland-urban interface
Forest Service and BLM staff who must meet goals and reporting duties
Timber companies and loggers
Electric utilities with rights-of-way on federal land
Livestock ranchers with grazing permits
Local governments and Indian tribes
Wildfire technology companies, nonprofits and universities
Wildlife, watersheds and recreation users in currently roadless national forest areas
Environmental groups that use lawsuits and public review to challenge projects

benefits: Higher, steady targets for thinning and prescribed fire could reduce fuel buildup and may lower wildfire risk near communities.
Public yearly reports and standard tracking could make federal fuel work easier to monitor.
Faster review for hazard tree removal and fast-track tools could speed up work in high-risk areas.
A technology pilot could test new tools for detecting and fighting fires.
Wider utility clearing near power lines could reduce the chance that trees spark outages or fires.
Local governments and tribes may have a stronger voice in projects that affect them.
concerns: Faster reviews and skipped environmental analysis could reduce public input and may miss effects on wildlife, water, or soil.
Raising the bidding-exemption limit could reduce competition and oversight in small timber sales.
Removing the 2001 Roadless Rule could open roadless areas to road building and logging, which may affect wildlife habitat, water quality, and recreation.
Expanded clearing near power lines could change habitat and scenic values.
Higher acreage targets could push agencies to meet numbers rather than focus on the most useful work, which is a possible risk.
Giving local governments and tribes a right to join lawsuits could lead to more litigation or delays for some projects, or could give them more influence, depending on the case.
Repealing the FLAME report removes one source of information on wildfire costs.
imp.cost: ["The material provided does not state the bill's total cost or any specific appropriation amounts. It requires cost-per-acre reporting in budget reports, but does not give cost figures."]
unknowns: The material does not say how much the bill would cost or where funding would come from.
It is not stated whether the agencies have enough staff or money to meet the higher acreage goals.
The effect of the 2021-2025 baseline depends on how many acres were treated in those years, which is not given.
It is unclear how often the fast-track review and skipped environmental review would be used, and how the 6,000-acre limit would work across projects.
The material does not say what the technology pilot would cost or what results it would produce.
It is not stated what the grazing study would find or whether grazing would be used.
The effect of the Roadless Rule repeal on specific areas is not described.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Reported by Senator Lee with an amendment in the nature of a substitute. Without written report.

crs:
This bill establishes forest management requirements for federal lands, particularly with respect to reducing wildfires. 
For example, the bill establishes annual goals to increase (1) the number of acres of Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land that are mechanically thinned (i.e., a management process related to the removal of trees and vegetation); and (2) the number of acres of Forest Service and BLM land treated by prescribed fire. By FY2029, the goals must be to increase the number of acres of each by at least 40% compared to the average number of acres of each in FY2019-FY2023.
The bill also directs the Forest Service and the BLM to (1) implement standardized procedures for tracking data relating to hazardous fuels reduction activities they carry out, and (2) develop a strategy to identify opportunities to use livestock grazing as a wildfire risk reduction tool on federal land. Additionally, the Forest Service and the Department of the Interior must establish a deployment and test bed pilot program for wildfire prevention, detection, communication, and mitigation technologies.
The bill mandates use of existing authorities for expedited environmental review for certain forest land at high risk from wildfire, insects, or disease.
Finally, the bill provides local governments and Indian tribes the right to intervene in lawsuits concerning certain projects on federal land that (1) reduce risks posed by wildfire, insects, or disease; or (2) generate revenue from harvesting timber.

news.overall: The evidence is extremely limited: only one Lean Left article (NPR headline, no description) was provided, and no coverage from other perspectives was included, so no cross-perspective comparison is possible. The headline does not explicitly connect the reported administrative action to the Wildfire Prevention Act, so the relationship between the two cannot be assessed from this input alone.

label: S. 1680
title: Virginia Wilderness Additions Act of 2025
one: The bill would add about 1,000 acres to the Rough Mountain Wilderness and about 4,600 acres to the Rich Hole Wilderness in Virginia's George Washington National Forest, allowing temporary use of motorized equipment on the Rich Hole land for water quality work before it becomes full wilderness.
summary:
This bill would protect more public forest land in western Virginia as wilderness. Wilderness is the strongest level of federal land protection. It generally bans roads, permanent buildings, and motor vehicles or machines.

About 1,000 acres would be added to the Rough Mountain Wilderness right away. The land is in the George Washington National Forest and is shown on a 2014 Forest Service map.

About 4,600 acres would be added to the Rich Hole Wilderness in two steps. First, the land becomes "potential wilderness," and the Forest Service must manage it under the Wilderness Act. The one exception is that the Forest Service may use motorized equipment and mechanized transport (such as machines or wheeled carts) to carry out water quality and fish passage projects. Those projects are described in a 2015 Forest Service decision called the Lower Cowpasture Restoration and Management Project. While doing this work, the agency must use the least intrusive tools it practically can.

The land becomes full wilderness on the earlier of two dates. One is when the Secretary of Agriculture publishes notice in the Federal Register that the work is done. The other is five years after the bill becomes law.

The bill does not say how much money it would cost, and it does not set aside new funding.
does: placeholder
who: Visitors who hike, hunt, fish, and camp in the George Washington National Forest
Nearby residents and local communities in western Virginia
The U.S. Forest Service, which manages the land
Wildlife, fish, and plants living in the affected forest and streams
People downstream who rely on the area's water quality
Timber, mining, and other commercial users who might otherwise seek access to the land
Mountain bikers and others who use mechanized equipment, who would be barred from the land once it is wilderness

benefits: Could protect about 5,600 acres of forest, wildlife habitat, and headwater streams from future development, road building, and logging.
Water quality and aquatic passage (fish and other aquatic life moving up and down streams) projects could be completed before the land becomes wilderness.
A fixed five-year deadline gives certainty that the land will be protected.
Requires the least intrusive tools for restoration work.
Has bipartisan Virginia support (both Virginia senators) and was reported out of committee without amendment.
concerns: Motorized equipment would be allowed in the area for up to five years, which could cause short-term disturbance to the land.
Wilderness status bars mechanized use such as mountain biking and limits some forest management, including fire and invasive species control, which some users and local officials may dislike.
The bill does not state whether local governments or residents were consulted. The text does not describe public input.
The bill does not describe how much of the restoration work is left or what it would cost.
imp.cost: The bill authorizes no new money. Any costs, such as the water quality work and land management, would come from existing Forest Service budgets. No cost estimate was provided in the material I saw.
unknowns: No CRS summary or Congressional Budget Office cost estimate was available.
I could not see the maps or the 2015 Lower Cowpasture decision, so I cannot confirm the exact work planned.
It is unclear how much of the restoration work is already finished.
The text does not describe local public input or how local stakeholders view the bill.

label: S. 1682
title: Alex Gate Safety Act of 2025
one: Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to make existing industry gate safety standards mandatory for large and vehicle gates within one year, and to run a national public education campaign about gate dangers.
summary: This bill would make gate safety rules mandatory. Right now, many gate safety standards are voluntary guidelines written by industry groups. The bill tells the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), the federal agency that handles dangerous consumer products, to issue a final safety rule within one year of the bill becoming law. The rule would require "covered gates" to meet certain existing standards from ASTM (a standards group) and, for gates with motors or similar operators, a standard called UL 325. Covered gates include automatic and manual vehicle gates and any other gate wider than 48 inches or 84 inches or taller. The CPSC would decide exactly which types of gates fall under the rule. If those standards groups update their standards, the update would automatically become part of the rule after 180 days unless the CPSC says within 90 days that the change does not improve safety. The CPSC could also change the rule later to reduce injury risk. Within two years, the CPSC must also launch a national campaign to teach manufacturers, contractors, owners, consumers, building officials, and school agencies about the dangers of falling or detached gates and about low-cost ways to prevent injuries. Within three years, it must report to Congress on what it did. The bill text does not state a dollar amount or any new money.

concerns: Manufacturers, installers, and owners could face added compliance costs, which might be passed on to consumers
Automatically adopting future industry-written standards means private groups can shape binding rules, with the CPSC only able to block changes that do not improve safety

The scope of covered gates is left to the CPSC, so the reach is uncertain

label: S. 1748
title: Kids Online Safety Act
one: Requires social media, online games, messaging apps and streaming services likely to be used by people under 17 to build in safety settings, parental tools, audits and reporting, and requires big platforms to let all users switch off personalized algorithms.
summary: This bill has two main parts. Title I covers apps and sites that kids under 17 are likely to use, such as social media, online games with chat or purchases, messaging apps, and video streaming. These companies must use "reasonable care" when designing features that keep kids hooked, to help prevent harms such as eating disorders, suicidal behavior, compulsive use, severe harassment, sexual exploitation, drug and gambling content, and deceptive money practices. They must give minors easy privacy and safety settings, set to the most protective option by default. They must also offer parents tools to see settings, limit time, and restrict purchases. Platforms must have a way to report harms and answer within 10 or 21 days, depending on size. They can't advertise drugs, tobacco, alcohol, cannabis, or gambling to known minors. They can't do market research on kids under 13, and need parental consent for teens. The largest social platforms must publish yearly independent audits. Title II applies to all users, not just kids. Large social platforms that tailor content using data users didn't knowingly provide must disclose how the algorithm works, and must let users switch to a version that doesn't use that data. The FTC and state attorneys general enforce it. Most rules start 18 months after enactment; the algorithm rules start after 1 year. I could only see the introduced text. The committee approved a revised version I could not read.
does: Requires covered platforms to use reasonable care in designing features (like infinite scroll, autoplay, push alerts, in-game purchases) to prevent listed harms to minors under 17.

Requires easy-to-use safeguards for known minors: limit who can contact them, hide their data, limit addictive features, opt out of personalized recommendations, restrict location sharing, and set time limits.
Makes the most protective settings the default for known minors unless a parent changes them.
Requires parental tools to view settings, restrict purchases, and see and limit time spent; for kids under 13 parents can change settings and tools are on by default.
Requires a reporting channel and a substantive response within 10 days (platforms over 10 million US monthly users) or 21 days (smaller ones), faster for imminent threats.
Bans facilitating ads for drugs, cannabis, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to known minors, and bans "dark patterns" that undermine safety or parental controls.
Requires ad labels, plain-language disclosures about recommendation systems, and resources for parents and minors.
Requires large social platforms (over 10 million US monthly users) to publish annual independent third-party audit reports on risks to minors and how well safeguards work.
Bans market or product research on children under 13 and requires verifiable parental consent for ages 13 to 16.
Orders a study on device-level or operating-system age verification, due 1 year after enactment, and FTC guidance within 18 months.
Creates an 11-member Kids Online Safety Council to advise Congress. It must report within 3 years and is exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act open-meeting rules.

Title II: starting 1 year after enactment, online platforms using "opaque" algorithms (based on data users didn't give for that purpose) must give notice, explain the main inputs and what the algorithm optimizes, and let users switch to an "input-transparent" algorithm at no extra cost. Trade secrets are protected from disclosure.

Enforcement is by the FTC and, for sections 103 to 105, state attorneys general. State attorneys general can't enforce the duty of care (section 102) under state law. There is no private right to sue in the text I saw.
Preempts only conflicting state laws and lets states pass stronger protections for minors.
who: Children and teens under 17 who use social media, games, messaging and streaming
Parents and guardians
Social media, gaming, messaging and streaming companies, especially those with over 10 million US monthly users
All adult users of large social platforms (algorithm choice under Title II)
FTC and state attorneys general
Schools, which receive the tools instead of students when a platform works on a school's behalf
Independent auditors and researchers

benefits: Minors may get stronger privacy and safety protections by default.
Parents may have more tools to monitor and manage a child's online use and spending.
Reporting and response requirements may make it easier to raise and address harms.
Limits on advertising and research on children may reduce exposure to certain marketing and data collection.
Users of personalized feeds may gain more information about how content is chosen and an option to avoid data-based personalization.
concerns: The phrase "reasonable care" and the list of harms are broad, so it is unclear how companies and regulators would apply them.
Companies may need to change product designs, which could affect how features work for minors and adults.
Age-related duties could lead platforms to collect more information to determine who is a minor.
Requirements for audits, reporting, and parental tools could add compliance costs for platforms.
Limits on features and content may affect free expression and access to information for some users, though the material does not say this directly.
imp.cost: ["The material provided does not state the bill's cost or how it would be funded."]
unknowns: This analysis is based only on the introduced text. The committee approved a revised version that was not available, so the final provisions may differ.
The material does not define key terms such as "reasonable care" or say how platform size is measured for the 10- and 21-day response rules.
It is not stated how platforms would verify whether a user is a minor.
The material does not say how much compliance would cost or how enforcement would be funded.
Current status is out of committee and on the Senate calendar; whether it will receive a floor vote is not stated.

crs:
Kids Online Safety Act
This bill requires covered online platforms, including social media platforms, to implement tools and safeguards to protect users and visitors under the age of 17. 
Covered platforms
 are online platforms, video games, messaging applications, or video streaming services used or likely to be used by individuals under the age of 17, with specified exceptions. 
The bill generally requires covered platforms to exercise reasonable care in the design and use of features that increase minors’ online activity in order to prevent and mitigate harm to minors (e.g., mental health disorders and severe harassment).  
Covered platforms are also required to provide certain safeguards to minors, such as protections for minors’ data; tools for parents of minors, such as access to minors’ privacy settings; and a mechanism for account holders and visitors to report harm to minors on the platform. 
Covered platforms are prohibited from conducting market or product research on children under the age of 13, and may only conduct such research on those under the age of 17 with parental consent. 
The bill provides for enforcement through the Federal Trade Commission and states. 
The bill also requires online platforms to meet certain requirements before using algorithms that select, order, or prioritize information presented to users based on user-specific data not provided for that purpose. Specifically, such platforms must (1) provide users with notice of the use of such algorithms, and (2) permit users to switch to an algorithm that does not rely on such user-specific data.

life.reason: Requires platforms to use reasonable care to prevent harms to minors such as suicidal behavior, eating disorders, sexual exploitation, and compulsive use, and adds protective defaults and reporting channels.

transparency.reason: Requires public annual independent audits of large platforms, plain-language disclosure of how recommendation algorithms work, ad labels, and parental visibility into minors' settings, though trade secrets are shielded and the committee-revised version was not reviewed.

people_over_profit.reason: Limits engagement-driven design, targeted advertising to minors, and market research on kids, and lets adults switch off data-driven algorithms, which constrains profit-maximizing practices in favor of user wellbeing.

honesty_kindness.reason: Bans dark patterns that undermine safety or parental controls and deceptive money practices aimed at kids, which promotes honest dealing with users, though the bill's effect on honesty overall is indirect.

news.overall: Coverage of the Kids Online Safety Act is sparse, with only one headline per group at most in the Center and Lean Left groups and three from Lean Right, so conclusions are tentative. Lean Left and Center coverage treats the bill as part of a political or legislative story, while Lean Right coverage focuses on litigation and speech issues, mostly around state-level rules and court orders rather than the federal bill itself. Only the Center headline names the bill's legislative path directly, and none of the headlines provided describe the bill's specific provisions.

label: S. 1759
title: Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
one: As reported by the Senate Commerce Committee, the bill tells the FAA to write a final rule within 2 years creating a noise-based certification standard for civil supersonic (faster-than-sound) aircraft, replacing the original text that would have lifted the overland supersonic ban whenever no sonic boom reaches the ground.
summary:
This bill is about passenger and business jets that fly faster than the speed of sound (supersonic). Today, FAA rules generally ban civil aircraft from flying supersonic over U.S. land unless they get a special authorization. The bill was introduced to change that, and the CRS summary describes that original version: allow supersonic flight without special authorization as long as no sonic boom reaches the ground.

The Senate Commerce Committee rewrote the bill before sending it to the full Senate. The version now on the Senate calendar does something different. It gives the FAA two years after enactment to issue a final rule that creates a "noise-based certification standard" for civil supersonic aircraft. The FAA must consult NASA. Takeoff and landing noise for these aircraft could not exceed the levels required of subsonic aircraft now in operation. The FAA must also set up a process to review and update the standards over time. The reviews would take into account better noise-reduction technology, research on sonic booms and acceptable sound levels, and changes in other rules.

The rewritten text does not mention emissions, fuel use, or public input beyond the normal rulemaking process. It also does not say outright whether supersonic flight over land is allowed or what boom level would be acceptable. Those details would be left to the FAA's rule.
does: Requires the FAA to issue a final rule within 2 years of enactment creating a noise-based certification standard for civil supersonic aircraft.
Requires the FAA to consult with NASA while writing the rule.
Sets takeoff and landing noise limits for these aircraft at no higher than what subsonic aircraft in operation must meet at the time of enactment.
Requires a process to review and update the takeoff and landing noise standards as technology and international standards change.
Requires a process to review and update the overall standard using new research on sonic booms and acceptable sound levels.
Replaces the original text, which would have had the FAA allow supersonic flight without special authorization as long as no sonic boom reaches the ground.
who: Aircraft makers and airlines developing or planning to use supersonic jets
People living near airports and under possible supersonic flight routes
The FAA and NASA, which would write and inform the rule
Air travelers, especially premium and business travelers
Communities, wildlife, and ecosystems exposed to aircraft noise and emissions

benefits: A clear noise-based standard could give aircraft makers a defined path toward certification.
Requiring takeoff and landing noise at or below current subsonic levels may limit noise near airports.
Periodic reviews could let the standard keep pace with new noise-reduction technology and research.
concerns: The rewritten bill does not say whether sonic booms over land would be allowed, so residents' exposure is unclear.
Emissions and fuel use are not addressed in the rewritten text.
The text mentions no public input beyond the normal rulemaking process.
Because key details are left to the FAA, the final outcome could differ from what the original bill described.
imp.cost: ["The material does not state any cost, funding amount, or budget impact for the bill."]
unknowns: Whether supersonic flight over U.S. land would be permitted under the rewritten bill.
What sonic boom level, if any, would be acceptable.
What the FAA's final rule would say, and how long it would take beyond the two-year deadline.
How the noise standard would be measured and enforced.
Effects on emissions, fuel use, airport communities, and the aviation industry.
Whether the bill will pass the full Senate or be enacted.

crs:
Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
This bill directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to allow civil aircraft to operate at speeds above Mach 1 (i.e., supersonic) over land in the United States under certain conditions.
Specifically, the FAA must issue or revise regulations to allow for the operation of civil aircraft at speeds greater than Mach 1 in the national airspace system without a special authorization, so long as no sonic boom reaches the ground in the United States.
Current regulations prohibit civil aircraft from operating above Mach 1 speeds over land in the United States without a special flight authorization issued by the FAA.

life.reason: Allowing supersonic aircraft under a noise-based standard that matches today's subsonic limits could increase noise exposure for people, wildlife, and ecosystems near routes, and the bill sets no boom or emissions limits.

air.reason: The bill does not address emissions or fuel use, and supersonic jets generally burn more fuel and emit more pollutants per passenger, so it could worsen air quality with no protection written in.

transparency.reason: The bill requires a rulemaking with the normal public process but adds no new disclosure or public input requirements, so its effect on transparency is unclear.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill mainly advances aircraft makers' and airlines' plans for faster premium service, with the public's noise and emissions burdens left unaddressed.

local_say.reason: By leaving boom levels and overland routes to a federal rule without requiring local input, the bill reduces communities' say over noise they would bear.

news.overall: Coverage volume is uneven: the Lean Left group has one headline, so its framing is thinly supported. The Center group has five headlines that focus heavily on the $50 billion funding request, its congressional pushback, and its political timing, while the Lean Left headline focuses on a negotiated safety overhaul deal. Descriptions are missing for all items, so the comparison rests on headlines alone and may miss nuance in the articles.

label: S. 1876
title: Stratton Ridge Air Force Memorial Act
short_title: Stratton Ridge Air Force Memorial Act
one: Lets the Forest Service allow a memorial for nine Air Force crew members killed in a 1982 crash to be moved from private land to a rest area on the Cherohala Skyway in North Carolina, at no federal cost.
summary: This bill deals with a memorial honoring nine Air Force crew members who died when a C-141B transport plane crashed over the Cherokee and Nantahala National Forests in North Carolina on August 31, 1982. The memorial now sits on private land next to the Cherohala Skyway, a scenic road. If the private landowner agrees, the bill lets the Secretary of Agriculture (who oversees the Forest Service) approve moving the memorial to the Stratton Ridge rest area at mile marker 2 of the Skyway, in Graham County, inside the Nantahala National Forest. The Secretary would do this through a "special use authorization," which is a permit for using national forest land. The exact spot must be approved by the North Carolina Department of Transportation. If the spot is next to a federal-aid highway, the Federal Highway Administration must also approve. No federal money may be used to move, install, or maintain the memorial. Whoever asks for the move must pay all costs, including the application review, any environmental review, and the moving and upkeep. The permit can include conditions, such as a ban on making the memorial bigger. The bill says "may," so it allows the move but does not require it.
does: Allows the Agriculture Secretary to permit the memorial to be installed at the Stratton Ridge rest area, mile marker 2 of the Cherohala Skyway, Graham County, NC.
who: Families, friends and fellow service members of the nine crew members

benefits: Could move the memorial to a public site that may be easier for visitors to reach, since it would sit at an existing rest area.
Could place the memorial on public land under Forest Service permit conditions, which may help with long-term care.
Requiring the requester to pay costs may shield taxpayers from expenses.
concerns: Moving the memorial would depend on the private landowner agreeing, so the move may not happen even if the bill passes.
Requiring the requester to pay all costs could make the move expensive for families or groups who want it.
Approval steps from several agencies could slow or complicate the process.
imp.cost: ["The bill says no federal money may be used to move, install, or maintain the memorial.", "The requester must pay all costs, including application review, any environmental review, and the moving and upkeep costs.", "The bill does not state a specific dollar amount for these costs."]
unknowns: The material does not say how much the move would cost or who would pay beyond the requester.
It is not stated whether the private landowner has agreed to the move.
The material does not describe what conditions the Forest Service might set beyond the example of banning enlargement.
It is not stated how the memorial would be maintained after the move or who would be responsible for it.
The material does not say whether the Stratton Ridge site is next to a federal-aid highway, which would trigger extra Federal Highway Administration approval.
The bill's current status is listed as out of committee and on the Senate calendar; whether it will pass is not stated.

crs:
Stratton Ridge Air Force Memorial Act
This bill authorizes the Forest Service to relocate a memorial in North Carolina honoring the nine Air Force crew members who lost their lives in an airplane crash in the Cherokee and Nantahala National Forests during a training mission on August 31, 1982, if the owner of the private land where the memorial is currently located consents. The Forest Service may relocate the memorial to an appropriate site at the Stratton Ridge rest area located at mile marker 2 on the Cherohala Skyway in Graham County, North Carolina, in the Nantahala National Forest. The site must be approved by (1) the North Carolina Department of Transportation, and (2) the Federal Highway Administration if the site is located adjacent to a federal-aid highway.

life.reason: The bill honors nine crew members who died in a crash, a memorial to lives lost, though it does not directly protect life.

local_say.reason: The move requires the private landowner's consent and state DOT and federal approvals, so local say is neither clearly advanced nor reduced.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill bars federal funds and requires the requester to pay all costs, so no bailout or ratepayer-funded tax break is involved.

honesty_kindness.reason: Relocating a memorial to a more accessible public rest area honors the families and fellow service members with a respectful tribute.

label: S. 2440
title: A bill to direct the Secretary of Agriculture to convey certain National Forest System land located in Franklin County, Mississippi, and for other purposes.
short_title: Okhissa Lake Rural Economic Development Land Conveyance
one: The bill would require the Forest Service to sell about 310 acres of surface land near Okhissa Lake in Homochitto National Forest, Mississippi, to a state agency for fair market value. The state agency would take on dam upkeep and safety duties, and the sale would be exempt from environmental review.
summary:
This bill would make the Secretary of Agriculture sell two pieces of Homochitto National Forest land in Franklin County, Mississippi, to the Scenic Rivers Development Alliance. The Alliance is an instrumentality (a body) of the State of Mississippi. The pieces are about 137.7 acres and about 173 acres, and they sit around Okhissa Lake. Only the surface of the land would transfer. The federal government would keep all minerals, oil, gas, and other underground rights.

The Alliance would pay cash equal to the land's fair market value, set by a federal-standard appraisal. It would also pay appraisal, survey, and closing costs. It would sign an agreement to pay for upkeep of the Okhissa Lake Dam and take responsibility for following federal and state dam safety laws. The sale money would go into a Forest Service fund used to buy other land for national forests.

The government would keep road and trail easements so the public can still reach the lake and nearby forest. It could take the land back if the land goes to a private (nonpublic) owner or is used for anything other than public recreation and fish and wildlife habitat. The Alliance could not split the land into home lots.

However, the bill says the Forest Service does not have to follow the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) or any other environmental law for the sale. The Forest Service would also not have to clean up any hazardous materials on the land. It would only have to disclose them. If the government takes the land back, the Alliance stays liable for cleanup.
does: Orders the Forest Service to convey about 137.7 acres and about 173 acres of surface land in Homochitto National Forest to the Scenic Rivers Development Alliance by quitclaim deed.
who: Scenic Rivers Development Alliance, the Mississippi state body that would receive the land and the dam duties

benefits: The Alliance could take over management of the lake area and dam, which may ease the federal government's upkeep duties.
Sale proceeds would go to a Forest Service fund for buying other national forest land.
Public road and trail easements would keep access to the lake and forest in place.
The reversion clause could keep the land in public recreation and wildlife use.
concerns: Skipping NEPA and other environmental review means the public may have less chance to weigh in on or learn about likely effects of the sale.
Not requiring hazardous material cleanup could leave contamination for future owners or the state to address.
Transferring the dam's upkeep may raise questions about whether the Alliance has enough funding to keep it safe over time.
Selling public land out of federal ownership may reduce long-term public control over the area.
imp.cost: ["The Alliance would pay cash equal to fair market value, as set by a federal-standard appraisal, plus appraisal, survey, and closing costs.", "Payments would go to a Forest Service fund used to acquire other land for the National Forest System.", "The bill does not state the appraised value or the total dollar amount of the sale.", "The bill does not state the expected cost of dam repairs or upkeep."]
unknowns: The appraised value of the land and the final sale price are not stated.
The condition of the Okhissa Lake Dam and the cost of its future upkeep are not stated.
The type and extent of any hazardous materials on the land are not described beyond a required disclosure.
It is not stated how the Alliance would fund its obligations or whether it would later sell or change use of the land.
The bill's current status is listed only as out of committee and on the Senate calendar; whether it will pass is unknown.

stage.last_action: Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. Reported by Senator Boozman with an amendment in the nature of a substitute. Without written report.

life.reason: The bill waives NEPA and other environmental review for the sale and removes the federal duty to clean up hazardous materials, only requiring disclosure, which weakens safeguards for people, wildlife, and plants on the land.

water.reason: Exempting the sale from environmental laws and leaving hazardous-material cleanup to disclosure only could allow contamination of waters around Okhissa Lake to go unaddressed, though the Alliance takes on dam safety duties that partly offset this.

transparency.reason: Waiving NEPA removes the public environmental review and disclosure process that normally informs people about federal land decisions, though hazardous-material disclosure is required.

local_say.reason: Transferring federal forest land out of federal management and waiving NEPA's public-input process reduces the public's say over the land, though reversion and recreation-use conditions preserve some local interest.

label: S. 277
title: A bill to release a Federal reversionary interest and convey mineral interests in Chester County, Tennessee, and for other purposes.
short_title: Chester County Church Encroachment Land Release Bill
one: The bill would have the federal government give up its future claim on, and its underground mineral rights to, a 0.62-acre piece of Chickasaw State Forest in Tennessee so a church that sits about 19 inches over the property line is no longer a problem.
summary: In 1955 the U.S. Forest Service gave a small piece of land in Henderson, Tennessee, to the state. That land is now part of Chickasaw State Forest. The federal government kept a "reversionary interest," which is a right to take the land back if the state stops using it for public purposes. The government also kept the mineral rights, meaning the rights to what lies underground. A recent state survey found that Bethel Baptist Church extends about 19 inches onto this 0.62-acre parcel. This bill would fix that problem by having the Secretary of Agriculture release the federal right to take the land back, with no payment. It would also hand over the federal mineral rights to Tennessee by quitclaim deed. A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the seller has, with no promises about its quality. The state would have to pay the federal government's administrative costs. The bill says these steps must happen without an appraisal, a mineral survey, or an environmental review. The bill does not itself say how the church's encroachment would be resolved after that. That would be up to the state. The bill would take effect once it becomes law. The text gives no timeline.
does: Directs the Secretary of Agriculture to release, without payment, the federal right to take back the 0.62-acre parcel if it stops being used for public purposes.
who: Bethel Baptist Church and its members in Henderson, Tennessee

benefits: The church's boundary problem may be cleared up, since the federal right to reclaim the land would no longer apply.
The state would gain full federal mineral rights to the parcel, which may simplify future management of the land.
Skipping appraisal and review may make the transfer faster and less costly to carry out, according to the bill's text.
concerns: Because the conveyance is a quitclaim with no warranty, the state receives no guarantee about the quality of the federal title or mineral rights.
Skipping an appraisal means the bill does not establish the land's or minerals' value, so the fairness of the no-payment terms is not checked.
Skipping environmental review means any environmental effects of the transfer are not assessed under this bill.
The bill does not say how the church's encroachment will be settled, so the boundary issue may remain unresolved after the transfer.
imp.cost: ["The bill requires the state of Tennessee to pay the Forest Service's administrative costs for the release and conveyance. The bill does not state the amount of these costs.", "The bill provides no appropriation and no payment for the land or minerals. The release is described as having no payment (no consideration)."]
unknowns: The bill does not say how much the administrative costs will be or how they will be calculated.
The bill does not say how the church's encroachment will be resolved after the transfer.
The bill does not state a timeline for completing the release and conveyance.
The bill's text does not say what the value of the mineral interests is, or whether they have any known mineral resources.
The bill does not describe any environmental conditions on the parcel.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. Reported by Senator Boozman without amendment. Without written report.

crs:
This bill provides for the transfer of the Forest Service's interest in the approximately 0.62-acre parcel of land within the Chickasaw State Forest to the state of Tennessee in order to resolve the encroachment of Bethel Baptist Church on that parcel. Both the parcel and the church are located in Chester County, Tennessee.
On August 12, 1955, the Forest Service conveyed the parcel to the state but retained a reversionary interest in the land that takes effect if the state forest land ceases to be used for public purposes. The bill directs the Forest Service to release the reversionary interest to the state.
Additionally, the Forest Service must convey to the state its mineral interest in the parcel. The conveyance must be done by quitclaim deed and without warranty or consideration (such as payment).
As a condition of the release and the conveyance, the state must pay for any administrative costs incurred by the Forest Service in carrying out the release and conveyance. The Forest Service must release the reversionary interest and convey the parcel without undertaking any appraisal, environmental review, or other report.

transparency.reason: The bill waives the appraisal, mineral survey, and environmental review, so the public gets less documentation about the land and mineral transfer.

label: S. 2970
title: A bill to authorize the use of off-highway vehicles in certain areas of the Capitol Reef National Park, Utah.
short_title: Capitol Reef Off-Highway Vehicle Access Bill
one: The bill would make Utah state law, not federal park rules, decide how cars, trucks, and off-highway vehicles (OHVs) can be used on 12 named roads inside Capitol Reef National Park.
summary: Capitol Reef National Park in Utah is run by the National Park Service. Federal park rules now generally control which vehicles can drive on park roads. This bill would change that for 12 named roads, or the parts of them inside the park boundary. They are Burr Trail Road, Cathedral Road, Hartnet Road, Highway 24, Notom Bullfrog Road, Polk Creek Road, Oil Well Bench Road, Baker Ranch Road, South Desert Overlook Road, Temple of the Sun and Moon Road, Gypsum Sinkhole Road, and Sulphur Creek Road. On those road sections, Utah state law would apply to the use of motor vehicles, including OHVs. The bill says an "off-highway vehicle" means whatever Utah law says it means. In practice, this could allow OHVs such as ATVs and side-by-sides on park road sections where they may not be allowed today. That depends on Utah's rules. The Senate committee made one small change. It specified that Baker Ranch Road is covered in Sevier and Wayne Counties. The bill does not give money, set any new safety or environmental rules, or require any study or public comment. It does not say how it interacts with other federal park protections. I could not see how park rules apply today, because that is not in the bill text.
does: Names 12 roads, and only the parts inside Capitol Reef National Park, as "covered roads."
Says Utah state law applies to motor vehicle use, including OHVs, on those road sections.
Uses Utah's own legal definition of "off-highway vehicle."
Through the committee amendment, specifies that Baker Ranch Road is covered in Sevier and Wayne Counties.
Does not include any funding, environmental review, public comment step, or limits on where OHVs can go.
who: OHV riders and other drivers who use roads in and around Capitol Reef
Residents and ranchers in Wayne and Sevier Counties who rely on these roads
National Park Service staff who manage the park and its roads
Wildlife, plants, soils, and archaeological sites along these corridors
Hikers, campers, and other visitors who value quiet and clean air
Local tourism businesses
Taxpayers across the country, who co-own national parks

benefits: Could give OHV riders clearer access to certain park road sections, depending on what Utah law allows.
Could align rules on these roads with state law, which may be simpler for some users to follow.
Could expand recreation options in the area for people who use off-highway vehicles.
concerns: Allowing OHVs on park road sections where they may not be allowed now could affect park scenery, quiet, and visitor experience.
Because the bill sets no new safety or environmental rules, it may leave certain impacts unaddressed.
Without a stated link to federal park protections, it may be unclear which rules apply on these roads, which could lead to confusion or disputes.
Public comment and studies are not required, so local or park concerns may not be formally considered before changes take effect.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not provide any money or set up any funding. The text does not state any cost estimate."]
unknowns: What current National Park Service rules say about vehicle use on these 12 road sections is not stated in the bill text.
What Utah law allows for OHVs on these roads, and whether it would permit them, depends on Utah rules that are not described in the bill.
How the bill would work with other federal park protections, such as resource or wildlife rules, is not stated.
Whether the change would affect park visitors, wildlife, or nearby land use is not described.
The bill's exact effect on enforcement, insurance, and liability is not addressed.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Reported by Senator Lee with an amendment in the nature of a substitute. Without written report.

crs: This bill makes the state law of Utah applicable to the use of motor vehicles (including off-highway vehicles) on the portions of each of Burr Trail Road, Cathedral Road, Hartnet Road, Highway 24, Notom Bullfrog Road, Polk Creek Road, Oil Well Bench Road, Baker Ranch Road, South Desert Overlook Road, Temple of the Sun and Moon Road, Gypsum Sinkhole Road, and Sulphur Creek Road that are located within the boundaries of the Capitol Reef National Park in Utah.

life.reason: Allowing OHVs on 12 park road corridors could disturb wildlife, plants, soils, and archaeological sites, though the bill itself sets no new protections and the effect depends on Utah rules.

one: The bill would require the Forest Service to give a small (about 0.81-acre) parcel in Perryville, Arkansas, to Perry County for free, to be used for public purposes like education and youth development.
summary: This bill would make the U.S. Forest Service hand over a small piece of land to Perry County, Arkansas. The land is about 0.81 acres at 1069 Fourche Avenue in Perryville, and it includes any buildings on it. The county has to ask for it in writing within 180 days after the bill becomes law. The county would not pay for the land itself, but it would have to pay all costs of the transfer. Those costs include a land survey, any environmental review required by federal law, and any review needed under the National Historic Preservation Act. The land would be given by quitclaim deed, which means the government passes along whatever interest it has but does not promise the title is clean. The Forest Service also would not have to provide the usual warranty or promise about environmental cleanup that normally applies when the government transfers property. The county could use the land only for public purposes, such as education and youth development. If the county stops using it that way, the Forest Service may choose to take it back. The Forest Service can also add other terms it considers necessary to protect the government's interests. The transfer is subject to any valid existing rights others have in the land.

label: S. 3226
title: Bring Our Heroes Home Act
one: Creates a public records collection at the National Archives and a five-member independent board to push federal agencies to release records about missing U.S. service members and civilians since December 7, 1941, with a presumption that the records be declassified.
summary:
This bill would set up a special "Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Collection" at the National Archives. It covers government records about U.S. troops and certain civilians (including some contractors) who went missing from December 7, 1941 to the date the bill becomes law. Federal agencies, the Library of Congress, and the Archives would have to search for these records, certify under penalty of perjury that they searched, and send copies to the Archives. Records cannot be destroyed or altered. The bill starts from the idea that these records should be made public. Agencies that want to withhold or heavily black out a record must publicly explain the specific harm and show it outweighs the public's interest.

A five-member independent Review Board, appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, would review requests to keep records secret. It could subpoena documents, hold hearings, and overrule an agency. The President can override the Board's decision on records created inside the executive branch, but must give a written, public reason. After 10 years, records must be fully released unless the President certifies that continued secrecy is necessary. Secrecy is still allowed for things like protecting sources, intelligence methods, active war plans, personal privacy, and active case work by the POW/MIA agency. The Board ends about four years after members are sworn in. The Senate committee amendment replaced the original authorization of funds with a statement that no additional funds are authorized.

one: The bill would remove "wilderness study area" protection from about 104,000 acres of federal land in Montana across three areas and require them to be managed under existing agency land plans instead.
summary: This bill would end the "wilderness study area" status of three pieces of public land in Montana. A wilderness study area is land that is kept in its natural state while Congress decides whether to make it permanent wilderness. The effects depend on what the current plans allow, such as roads, logging, motorized use, or other development.

title: National Quantum Initiative Reauthorization Act of 2026
short_title: National Quantum Initiative Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Renews and expands the federal quantum technology research program through 2034, adding new research centers, testbeds, workforce programs, supply chain studies, and security rules, while ending the National Nanotechnology Program.
summary: This bill renews a federal program that coordinates research on quantum technology. Quantum technology uses the laws of physics at the tiniest scales to build new kinds of computers, sensors, and communication networks. The bill extends the program's authority to the end of 2034 and sets spending levels for 2026 through 2030. It adds up to three new quantum centers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), doubles the National Science Foundation (NSF) research centers from 5 to 10, and creates testbeds where new quantum uses can be tried out. It also creates a national workforce hub with community colleges, new student training and fellowship options, and a NASA quantum program. It directs studies of quantum supply chains, a plan for working with allies, and a review of regulations that may slow quantum work. It pushes the government and businesses toward "post-quantum" encryption, which is designed to stay secure against future quantum computers. It bars certain funds from going to Confucius Institute–linked schools or to research with countries and groups of concern, and adds research-security screening. It requires yearly outside evaluations of the program, with a public summary. Finally, it shuts down the National Nanotechnology Program 180 days after enactment. Most dollar amounts are "authorizations," meaning limits on what Congress may later fund, not actual spending.

one: As reported by the Senate committee, the bill only defines "latest published editions" of building codes as the two most recent editions for FEMA's pre-disaster mitigation grants; the loan-fund change and home retrofit pilot in the original bill were cut.
summary:
This bill changes a federal disaster law, the Stafford Act, which covers how FEMA helps before and after disasters. The version reported out of committee on September 15, 2026 is much smaller than the version introduced in February 2025. The committee deleted everything after the enacting clause and replaced it with a short text.

What is left: FEMA's pre-disaster mitigation program gives money to states, tribes, and local governments to reduce future disaster damage. That law refers to the "latest published editions" of building codes and standards. The bill would define that phrase as the two most recently published editions, meaning the current edition or the one before it. A government that has adopted the previous edition would not be treated as behind. The bill also says it should not be read to affect any other program.

What was removed: The original bill would also have stopped states from using the Safeguarding Tomorrow revolving loan fund for building-code work. It would also have set up a pilot program, ending in 2030, for grants to help people with financial need retrofit their homes against local hazards like floods, tornadoes, earthquakes, wildfires, and wind. It would have used up to 10% of annual pre-disaster mitigation funds. The CRS summary describes this original version, not the reported one. Those parts are not in the reported text I was given.

Promoting Resilient Buildings Act
This bill increases flexibility for predisaster mitigation assistance for building code activities, prohibits using certain loan funds for building code activities, and establishes a pilot program to fund residential resilience retrofits.
Under current law, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) may provide predisaster hazard mitigation assistance to government entities for implementing the latest published editions of relevant building codes and standards. Also, FEMA must consider a government entity’s adoption of such building codes when determining whether to award it predisaster hazard mitigation assistance. The bill specifies that the building codes applicable in such instances are the two most recently published editions (i.e., either the current edition or the previous one).
Also, currently, under FEMA's Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund (STRLF) program, states and Indian tribal governments may provide loans to local governments for establishing and carrying out building codes and standards. The bill removes this authority, so STRLF loans may not be used for such building code-related activities.
Additionally, the bill establishes a pilot program for FEMA to provide grants to government entities that then provide the funding to individuals for residential resilience retrofits. The retrofit projects must reduce risk to homes from local natural hazards and individuals must demonstrate financial need. To implement the pilot program, FEMA may use up to 10% of the funds FEMA provides annually for predisaster hazard mitigation assistance. The pilot program terminates at the end of FY2030.

label: S. 4116
title: Geo POWER Act
one: The bill would have the Department of Energy create a program that gives milestone-based financing to at least three next-generation geothermal power demonstration projects in at least three states, with up to $800 million authorized.
summary: This bill tells the Department of Energy (DOE) to set up a new program within 180 days of becoming law. The program would help pay for experimental geothermal power projects. Geothermal power uses heat from underground to make electricity. These projects would be in rock that water does not flow through easily, which needs newer drilling methods. Money would be awarded in stages, as a project hits technical and money-related goals. DOE would give priority to projects in places that have little or no geothermal power now, including on or near Indian land. It would also favor projects that share data publicly, projects aimed at 30 megawatts or more of power, and projects likely to attract private investment. DOE must fund at least 3 proposals, in at least 3 states, from at least 3 different sponsors. The Senate committee changed the bill to authorize $800 million, with up to $750 million for projects and up to $50 million for running and overseeing the program. An authorization only allows spending. Congress must still pass a separate law to provide the money. The bill also removes an existing part of the law, paragraph (3) of subsection (d) of section 615, and the text does not say what that paragraph covers. The bill text has no new environmental, water, or local-input rules. Existing laws would still apply.

label: S. 4410
title: A bill to amend the Mineral Leasing Act to provide for the payment of bonus payments of certain coal leases issued under that Act.
short_title: Coal Lease Bonus Payment Installments Bill
one: The bill would let companies that win federal coal leases under a deferred-payment system pay their upfront "bonus" bid in 10 equal yearly installments, with the first paid when they bid.
summary: When the federal government leases public land for coal mining, the winning company pays a "bonus bid." That is a one-time amount offered to win the lease, on top of later royalties (a share of the coal's value). The Mineral Leasing Act already allows a "deferred bonus payment" system, where the bonus can be paid over time. This bill sets the terms for that system. If a coal lease is issued under it, the bonus must be paid in 10 equal annual installments. The first installment is due with the bid, and the other nine come over the following years. The bill is one short paragraph added to the law. It doesn't change royalties, environmental rules, or how leases are offered. It doesn't say what happens if a company stops paying, and it doesn't say whether interest is charged. It also doesn't say whether the system is required or only allowed. The effect would be that coal companies pay less up front and the government gets its money later. The text has no cost estimate, and no Congressional Research Service summary is available yet. The bill was reported out of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee without changes. It is on the Senate calendar, and no vote has been scheduled.

concerns: The government would receive its bonus money later, over up to nine years, rather than at the time of the bid.

label: S. 465
title: GRID Power Act
one: The bill orders FERC to write rules letting power grid operators move "dispatchable" power plants (ones that can supply steady, predictable power on demand, which may include fossil fuel plants) ahead in the line to connect to the grid.
summary: New power plants must wait in a line, called the interconnection queue, before they can connect to the high-voltage electric grid. This bill would require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), the federal agency that oversees the interstate power grid, to change the rules for that line. Within 90 days of the bill becoming law, FERC must start writing new rules. The final rules are due within 180 days. The rules must let grid operators ask FERC for permission to move "dispatchable" projects higher in the line. Dispatchable means a power source that can provide known, predictable power when the grid needs it. The bill's text does not list which fuels count. The Congressional Research Service says it generally covers sources like fossil fuel plants. A grid operator that asks for this must show why it is needed and explain how it would improve reliability or resilience. It must also hold a public comment and stakeholder process before it submits the request, and it must report regularly to FERC on grid reliability. FERC would have 60 days to approve or deny each request. FERC would also have to review its rules at least every five years. The bill says nothing about costs, who pays, or what happens to projects pushed back in line, such as wind, solar, or some batteries.
does: Requires FERC to start a rulemaking within 90 days and finish final rules within 180 days of enactment.
Directs FERC to address inefficiencies in how interconnection requests are processed so new dispatchable projects can connect quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably.
Lets grid operators (transmission providers, including regional grid organizations) propose moving dispatchable projects that improve reliability and resource adequacy to higher places in the queue.
Requires each proposal to show a need for the prioritization and explain how it improves grid reliability or resilience.
Requires public comment and stakeholder engagement before a proposal goes to FERC.
Requires regular reports to FERC on grid reliability and resilience and on actions taken under the Act.
Gives FERC 60 days to approve or deny each proposal.
Requires FERC to review and, if needed, update the rules at least every five years.
who: Developers of new power plants waiting in interconnection queues (both dispatchable and non-dispatchable, such as wind and solar)
Grid operators, utilities, and regional transmission organizations
FERC staff, who would take on a fast rulemaking and 60-day reviews
Electricity customers and ratepayers, who pay for reliability and generation costs through their bills
Communities near new power plants and the people who breathe their emissions

benefits: Supporters may argue that prioritizing dispatchable power could help keep the grid reliable when demand is high or supply is tight.
Faster connection of dependable power sources could help grid operators plan for resource adequacy.
The bill requires public comment and reliability reporting, which may add transparency to queue changes.
concerns: Projects moved back in the queue, such as wind, solar, or some batteries, could face longer delays or added costs, though the bill does not address this.
Because the bill does not define which fuels count as dispatchable, the scope of priority projects is unclear and could be broad.
Critics may argue that favoring one type of generation could slow the addition of other clean power sources.
The 60-day FERC review and 180-day rulemaking deadlines are short for complex grid rules, which could raise questions about how thorough the review is.

Guaranteeing Reliability through the Interconnection of Dispatchable Power Act or the GRID Power Act
This bill requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to issue and periodically review a rule that revises the approval process for interconnection requests of generating units that produce electricity to prioritize dispatchable power projects (e.g., certain fossil fuel projects). 
Under the bill,
 d
ispatchable power
 generally refers to an electric energy generation resource, such as a generating unit that produces electricity from fossil fuels, capable of providing known and forecastable electric supply in time intervals necessary to ensure grid reliability. Currently, FERC receives interconnection requests from those projects and other generating units, such as units that produce electricity from renewable energy. Interconnection requests are requests from generating units to connect to the high voltage transmission lines of the electric grid.
First, the rule must address the efficiency and effectiveness of the existing procedures for processing interconnection requests to ensure that new dispatchable power projects that improve grid reliability and resource adequacy can interconnect to the electric grid quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably. 
Second, the rule must revise the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Procedures, and the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Agreement as appropriate, to authorize transmission providers to submit proposals to FERC to prioritize new dispatchable power projects that will improve grid reliability and resource adequacy by assigning those projects higher positions in the interconnection queue of the provider. FERC must review and approve or deny such proposals within 60 days after the proposal is submitted.

air.reason: Fast-tracking dispatchable projects, which the CRS says generally includes fossil fuel plants, while pushing back wind and solar could increase emissions from new generation.

transparency.reason: The bill requires public comment, stakeholder engagement, and reports to FERC, but these are offset by a short 60-day review and no explicit public disclosure of the prioritization decisions, so the net effect is unclear.

people_over_profit.reason: Expediting queue position for dispatchable projects mainly benefits developers of new plants, and the bill provides no safeguards against the profit interests of those developers.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide subsidies, bailouts, or tax breaks, but it is silent on who pays for the reliability and generation costs, so the effect is unclear.

label: S. 4709
title: UNLOCK AUKUS Act
one: The bill makes a one-line change to the Arms Export Control Act so that three specific exclusions no longer limit the license-free export of certain defense items to Australia and the United Kingdom under the AUKUS security partnership.
summary:
AUKUS is a security partnership among Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Under current law, some U.S. defense items and services can be sent to Australia and the UK without the usual individual export license. That shortcut has limits. This bill changes one of those limits.

The limit sits in Section 38(l)(4)(B) of the Arms Export Control Act. It refers to another part of the law, subsection (j)(1)(C)(ii). The bill adds the words "excluding subclauses (I), (II), and (III)" after that reference. In effect, three listed items in that other part would no longer count toward the limit.

The bill text does not say what those three items are. It also doesn't say how much easier or harder exports would become. The Congressional Research Service has not yet published a summary. I could not see the text of the section being referenced, so I can't say exactly which items or technologies are affected. The bill's title suggests the goal is to speed up licensing and technology sharing among the three countries. That is an inference from the name, not something the text says.

The bill has 10 cosponsors from both parties. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee reported it without changes, and it is now on the Senate calendar. The text sets no start date, no new spending, and no new reporting rules.
does: Amends Section 38(l)(4)(B) of the Arms Export Control Act by adding 'excluding subclauses (I), (II), and (III)' after the reference to subsection (j)(1)(C)(ii).
Narrows a limit on AUKUS license-free defense exports and transfers, so three listed items would no longer count toward that limit.
Gives the bill its short name, the UNLOCK AUKUS Act.
Adds no new funding, no new reporting rules, and no new penalties in the text provided.

concerns: Because the bill does not name the three items, it is hard to tell which technologies could move with less review.
Less licensing oversight for some items could raise questions about how sensitive technology is controlled, though the text does not say this will happen.

label: S. 4846
title: TAAP Act
short_title: TAAP Act (Transboundary Aquifer Assessment Program Act)
one: Renews and extends a federal program that studies groundwater shared between the U.S. and Mexico, adds Arizona aquifers to the study list (with one exception), and authorizes funding through fiscal year 2036.
summary:
Some underground water supplies, called aquifers, sit under both the United States and Mexico. A 2006 law set up a program to study these shared aquifers, working with states, universities, and Mexico. The program's funding permission ran out after 2016. This bill would renew it.

The bill does three things. First, it widens the list of states where "priority" aquifers can be picked for study. The current law covers New Mexico and Texas. The bill would add Arizona, but not the shared aquifer that is partly in the Yuma groundwater basin, which is excluded. Second, it says Congress may spend money on the program for fiscal years 2026 through 2036. Third, it resets the program's end date so the clock starts from when this new law is enacted instead of from 2006.

The bill does not set a dollar amount or change the other parts of the 2006 law. "Authorizing" funding only allows Congress to pay for the program. A separate spending bill would still have to provide the money. The bill text does not say why the Yuma-area aquifer is left out. The bill text does not give the new end date, because it refers to the existing law's timeline, which I could not see.
does: placeholder
who: Residents and water users in Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas border regions
Communities in northern Mexico (Sonora and other border states) that share these aquifers
Water agencies, state geological surveys, and universities that take part in the studies
The U.S. Geological Survey and other federal agencies that run the program
Taxpayers, since Congress would pay for the work

benefits: Better data on shared groundwater could help protect drinking water supplies for border communities.
Studies could improve cooperation between the U.S. and Mexico on shared water.
Research-focused work builds public, transparent data that communities and local governments can use.
concerns: The authorization has no dollar cap in this text, and actual money depends on later spending bills; a program without funding could stall.
The Yuma-area aquifer is excluded, and the bill text does not explain why, so that area may not get the same public study.
The bill covers assessment only; it does not itself protect water quality or limit pumping.

unknowns: The exact funding level per year under the underlying 2006 law.

label: S. 4870
title: Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Extends the federal Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (a USGS-led effort to map underground resources) for five more years (2027–2031), adds newer mapping technologies, and links it to the 3D Hydrography Program.
summary:
This bill would keep alive a federal program called the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, or Earth MRI. It was created in the 2021 infrastructure law and is run through the U.S. Geological Survey. The program collects maps and data about what is under the ground, with a focus on critical minerals, which are materials used in things like batteries and electronics. Its current authorization runs from 2022 through 2026. The bill changes that to 2027 through 2031.

The bill also updates the program's mapping purpose. It says the data may come from newer tools, such as airborne gravity gradiometry (measuring tiny changes in gravity from aircraft), digital geochemistry, real-time data collection, and data-driven analysis. These could help describe critical minerals, geothermal energy, geologic hydrogen, and other underground resources.

Finally, the bill adds the 3D Hydrography Program, a federal water-mapping effort, to the list of data sources the Earth MRI must combine with its own data.

The bill text we have does not give a dollar amount. It only extends the time period. Any money would depend on later spending decisions by Congress. The bill also does not add rules on environmental review, public input, or mining permits.
does: Extends the Earth MRI's authorization period from 2022–2026 to 2027–2031.
Says the program's mapping data may come from newer technologies, including airborne gravity gradiometry, digital geochemistry, real-time data collection, and data-driven analysis.
Adds geothermal, geologic hydrogen, and other underground resource systems to the resources the data may help describe, alongside critical minerals.
Adds the 3D Hydrography Program to the data sources the program must integrate.
Replaces the original bill text with a committee amendment; the main change is wording on the technology list and on adding "geologic hydrogen."

Newer mapping tools may produce more detailed information about critical minerals and other underground resources.
Combining Earth MRI data with the 3D Hydrography Program could make geologic and water data work together more closely.
concerns: The bill text does not give a dollar amount, so it is unclear whether the program would receive enough funding to use the extended time period fully.
The bill does not add rules on environmental review, public input, or mining permits, so the mapping data alone would not change those processes.
Mapping data could be used to support future mineral or energy development, which may raise environmental or land-use questions that the bill does not address.

label: S. 4950
title: ITS Codification Act
one: The bill writes the Commerce Department's Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (a federal radio and wireless test lab) into law and creates an initiative to develop technology for locating people trapped in mines, collapsed buildings, and similar places where radios don't work well.
summary: The Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS) is a federal lab that already exists inside the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), the part of the Commerce Department that advises on telecom and manages federal use of radio airwaves. This bill would put ITS into permanent law instead of leaving it to agency decisions alone. The law would say ITS serves as a lab for the executive branch. It would study radio signals, how they travel, and how they cause interference. It would also test technology that lets federal and non-federal users share airwaves, and it would study how well federal systems tolerate interference. ITS could also take on other tasks the NTIA head assigns. The bill lets ITS make agreements with companies, universities, and other agencies under existing laws on technology partnerships, interagency work, and patents and licensing. The second part requires ITS to start an initiative for emergency communication and tracking tools. These would help find people trapped in places such as underground mines, tall buildings, or collapsed structures. ITS would work with private companies and federal agencies to assess needs and help develop technical standards. Within 18 months, NTIA must send Congress a public report on that needs assessment. The bill does not state a dollar amount or new funding.
