label: H.R. 5068
title: MORE Act
short_title: MORE Act (Federal Cannabis Decriminalization and Expungement)
one: The bill would remove marijuana from the federal list of controlled substances, erase many past federal cannabis convictions, tax the cannabis industry, and use the tax money for grants and loans for communities harmed by the war on drugs.
summary: This bill would end the federal ban on marijuana. It takes marijuana and THC off the federal list of controlled substances and ends federal criminal penalties for growing, selling, or having it. The change would also apply to past cases. Federal courts would have one year to erase (expunge) non-violent federal cannabis convictions and related arrests. People still serving sentences could ask for a review hearing, and the court would resentence them as if the new law had applied. Poor defendants would get a lawyer. The bill adds a federal tax on cannabis products, starting at 5% of the sale price and rising to 8%. After five years, the tax would switch to a rate based on weight or THC content. It also adds a $1,000 yearly tax on each growing or warehouse site, plus federal permits and bonds. The tax money would go into an "Opportunity Trust Fund." That fund pays for community grants (job training, legal aid, reentry help, drug treatment), small business loans for disadvantaged owners, and grants to states that adopt fairer licensing rules. Cannabis businesses could also use Small Business Administration programs. Federal benefits, security clearances, and immigration status could not be denied because of cannabis use or past cannabis convictions. Federal employee drug testing and transportation safety testing could continue. The bill orders several studies on topics such as impaired driving, workplaces, schools, and public health. It authorizes $10 million for the impaired-driving study. Existing FDA authority is kept.
does: Removes marijuana and THC from the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules, with the change applying to past offenses and pending cases.
Orders the Attorney General to finish the rulemaking to deschedule within 180 days.
Requires federal courts to expunge non-violent federal cannabis convictions and related arrests within one year, with sealed records. People can also petition the court themselves.
Gives people currently serving sentences a sentencing review hearing, with appointed counsel if they are poor.
Excludes people who got an "aggravating role" (leader or organizer) adjustment at sentencing from expungement.
Creates a federal excise tax on cannabis products: 5% of the sale price in years 1–2, then 6%, 7%, and 8%. After year 5 it becomes a per-ounce or per-gram rate set at 8% of prevailing prices.

Adds a $1,000 yearly occupational tax per production or export warehouse site, plus federal bonds and permits, record-keeping, packaging and labeling rules, and civil and criminal penalties for tax evasion.

Creates the Opportunity Trust Fund: 50% for community reinvestment grants, 10% for substance use disorder services, 20% for SBA loans and technical help for disadvantaged-owned businesses, and 20% for SBA equitable licensing grants to states and localities.
Creates a Cannabis Justice Office in the Department of Justice to run the Community Reinvestment Grant Program for nonprofits.
Bars SBA programs and lenders from refusing service solely because a business is a state-legal cannabis business or service provider.
Bars denial of federal public benefits, and denial or loss of security clearances, based on cannabis use or cannabis convictions.
Stops cannabis from counting as a controlled substance for immigration purposes, and bars denial of immigration benefits for past cannabis conduct or convictions.
Lets federal employee drug testing and Department of Transportation and Coast Guard testing continue to cover marijuana.
Requires the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish demographic data on cannabis business owners and workers, with personal identifying information kept confidential.

Orders studies on state legalization's societal effects, impaired driving ($10 million authorized), workplaces, schools, and the demographics of those convicted. Requires an FDA public meeting on cannabis product safety and labeling.
Replaces the words "marijuana" and "marihuana" with "cannabis" throughout federal law.
People with federal cannabis convictions or arrests, and people now serving federal cannabis sentences
Immigrants facing deportation or denied benefits over cannabis offenses
Cannabis growers, processors, importers, and export warehouses, who would pay new federal taxes and follow federal permit rules
Small business owners who are socially and economically disadvantaged, and small cannabis businesses seeking SBA help
Nonprofits that provide reentry, legal aid, and treatment services
State and local governments that run licensing programs
Federal employees, transportation workers, and security clearance holders
Consumers of cannabis
Courts, the Department of Justice, Treasury/IRS, SBA, FDA, and the Department of Transportation
Could end federal arrests and prosecutions for cannabis. The bill's findings cite over 200,000 arrests per year and about $3.6 billion in enforcement costs, citing the ACLU.
Expungement and resentencing could remove barriers to jobs, housing, and benefits for people with old convictions.
Protects immigrants from deportation and benefit denials over cannabis.
Directs cannabis tax money to the communities most affected by past enforcement, rather than to general revenue.
Could improve access to loans and business help for small and disadvantaged operators.
Requires public data and reports (BLS demographics, GAO studies, Treasury methodology), which supports transparency.
Funds drug treatment and health education, and lets treatment services reach people with non-cannabis drug records.
Orders studies on impaired driving, schools, and workplace safety, and keeps federal drug testing in place.

Federal legalization could increase use, including among youth, and may add to impaired driving or health problems. The bill orders studies but does not set up its own federal regulatory system for these risks.
The bill keeps FDA authority but does not create a federal regulatory framework for product safety, potency, marketing, or testing. It only requires one public meeting.
The bill does not address environmental effects of cannabis cultivation, such as water and energy use. This could matter for a person who values clean water and clean air.
The bill does not give local communities a say. It does keep state and local laws in force, since paying the tax does not authorize operating against state or local law.
The bill's SBA provisions could put taxpayer-backed loan guarantees behind cannabis businesses, which creates some risk for taxpayers if loans default.
Large companies could dominate a legal national market, and the bill relies on grants and loans to counter that.
The new federal permit, bond, and tax system could be costly for small operators and could carry criminal penalties of up to 5 years for tax fraud.
Excluded from expungement are people with an aggravating role adjustment, and violent offenses are not covered.
who: People who grow, sell, or possess marijuana or THC products
People with past federal non-violent cannabis convictions or arrests, and people still serving federal cannabis sentences
Cannabis businesses, including growers, warehouses, and producers that would pay the new federal taxes and permit fees
Disadvantaged business owners who could receive Opportunity Trust Fund loans
Community organizations and individuals in areas affected by the war on drugs who could receive trust fund grants
State governments that could receive grants for adopting fairer licensing rules
Federal courts, which would handle expungements and resentencing requests
Applicants for federal benefits, security clearances, and immigration status
Federal employees subject to drug testing and transportation workers subject to safety testing

This bill decriminalizes marijuana.

requires the Bureau of Labor Statistics to regularly publish demographic data on cannabis business owners and employees,

label: H.R. 5468
title: Community College Agriculture Advancement Act of 2025
short_title: Community College Agriculture Advancement Act of 2025
one: The bill would let USDA give competitive grants to community colleges (and groups of them) to build up farm and natural resources training, education, research, and outreach, with up to $20 million a year authorized for 2026–2031.
summary: This bill would create a new grant program at the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) for community colleges and groups of two-year public colleges that support agriculture. Colleges would compete for the money. The grants would help them keep and grow their ability to offer job training, classes, research, and outreach on agriculture and similar fields. USDA must give priority to colleges that team up with a local farm or agriculture business to give students hands-on training. Colleges could use the money to buy equipment, pay for faculty development, set up apprenticeships and work-based learning, teach about farm jobs (including business subjects like accounting, paralegal studies, and finance), share information with the public, and improve their odds of winning other grants. "Authorizes" means Congress would still need to pass a separate spending bill to actually provide the money.

label: H.R. 598
title: FIR Act
one: The bill says the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management do not have to redo Endangered Species Act reviews of their long-term land plans when a new species is listed, new critical habitat is set, or new information shows harm not previously considered.
summary:
Federal agencies that manage public land, mainly the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), write long-term plans for how each forest or area will be used. Under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), they must consult with wildlife agencies to check that those plans won't harm protected species. Current rules say that this consultation must be reopened ("reinitiated") in certain cases. Those cases include a new species being listed, new critical habitat being designated, or new information showing the plan may harm a protected species in a way that wasn't looked at before.

This bill would change the laws that govern Forest Service and BLM planning. It would say that the agencies are not required to reopen consultation in those situations. The language begins "notwithstanding any other provision of law," so it would override the ESA and its regulation (50 CFR 402.16) on this point. The bill does not ban reconsultation. It only removes the requirement. It does not say what, if anything, would replace it, and it does not cover individual projects approved under the plans. The bill has no listed cost. It has been referred to a House subcommittee, and I could not see any further action.
does: Amends the Forest and Rangeland Renewable Resources Planning Act so the Forest Service need not reinitiate ESA consultation on forest plans when a new species is listed or critical habitat is designated.
Also removes the requirement when new information shows a plan may affect a listed species or critical habitat in a way or to an extent not previously considered.
Amends the Federal Land Policy and Management Act to give BLM the same exemption for its land use plans.
Uses 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' wording, so it would override ESA section 7(a)(2) and the regulation at 50 CFR 402.16 for these plans.
Makes no mention of funding, new monitoring, or other safeguards.
who: Forest Service and BLM planners and staff
Threatened and endangered species and their habitat on national forests and BLM land
Timber, grazing, mining, energy and recreation users of public lands
Local communities, tribes and the public who rely on or live near federal lands
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries (consulting agencies)
Conservation groups and others who bring lawsuits over land plans

benefits: Agencies could avoid repeating consultation when new species listings or habitat designations occur, which may save time and staff effort.
Land management plans may be easier to keep on schedule, since reopening consultation can take a long time.
Land managers may have more certainty about plans they have already approved.
concerns: Species listed or habitat designated after a plan is approved might not get a fresh review of the plan's effects, which could leave protected species less protected.
New scientific information about harm to a listed species might not lead to a new review, which could delay or prevent changes to the plan.
Because the bill overrides the Endangered Species Act on this point, it could weaken a standard set in federal law.
Because the bill does not replace the requirement, there may be no required check at all in these situations.
imp.cost: >The bill has no listed cost, and the material does not state any budget or funding effects.
unknowns: The material does not say what, if anything, would replace reconsultation.
It is not stated how the bill would affect individual projects approved under the plans, since the bill does not cover them.
It is not stated how often these situations arise or how many plans might be affected.
The material does not say whether the agencies or wildlife agencies would still be able to reconsult voluntarily.
The bill has been referred to a House subcommittee, and no further action was found, so its final form and chance of passage are unknown.

stage.last_action: Referred to the Subcommittee on Forestry and Horticulture.

crs:
Forest Information Reform Act or the FIR Act
This bill specifies that neither the Forest Service nor the Bureau of Land Management are required to reinitiate consultation on a land management plan when a new species is listed as threatened or endangered, critical habitat is designated, or new information reveals effects of the plan may affect a listed species or critical habitat in a manner or to an extent not previously considered.

life.reason: Removing the requirement to reopen ESA consultation when new species are listed, critical habitat is designated, or new harms emerge means land plans could keep harming protected wildlife and plants without federal wildlife agencies re-checking them.

water.reason: Forest and BLM land plans govern logging, grazing, mining and road activity that affect watersheds, and skipping reconsultation on new information could allow more water-quality harm in listed-species habitat.

transparency.reason: The bill removes a procedural check that requires agencies to revisit plans with new information, and it adds no replacement disclosure or public-review requirement, which reduces openness about how plans are updated.

people_over_profit.reason: The change mainly eases compliance burdens for timber, grazing, mining and energy interests that operate under these plans, at the expense of public and species protections.

local_say.reason: Communities and the public would lose the reconsultation trigger that helps address new information about local lands, and the bill offers no substitute opportunity for local input.

news.overall: Only three Lean Left headlines were provided, with no article descriptions, so the evidence is thin and based on headlines alone. The coverage centers on environmental and process concerns, and the descriptions are empty, so the analysis cannot confirm how the articles treat the bill's merits in detail.

label: H.R. 6192
title: Fertilizer Research Act of 2025
one: Requires the USDA to publish, within one year, a public report on the U.S. fertilizer industry covering prices, imports, market concentration, regulation, new fertilizer technologies, and price transparency.
summary: This bill would make the Secretary of Agriculture, working with the USDA's Economic Research Service, write and post a public report about the U.S. fertilizer industry. The report would be due one year after the bill becomes law. It would look at how the fertilizer industry affects the prices farmers get for their crops, and how big the fertilizer market has been over the last 25 years. It would also cover price patterns and where fertilizer comes from, including lists of imported fertilizer types, importing companies, and source countries. It would explain how anti-dumping and countervailing duties (extra taxes on unfairly cheap or subsidized imports) affect retail prices. The report would study whether a few companies control too much of the market and whether that has hurt competition. It would compare newer products, such as biological fertilizers, with conventional ones on price, efficiency, and yield. It would review the rules on making, distributing, and using fertilizer, including where they are seen as hurting domestic production. It would also judge whether public fertilizer price reporting is transparent enough. It would evaluate, and recommend to Congress on, a possible rule making industry report prices daily, weekly, or monthly. It would also look at expected market growth and risks. Confidential business information would be left out. The bill itself creates no new rules, fees, or programs.
does: Requires USDA to publish a fertilizer industry report on its website within one year of enactment.
Requires the report to cover market size, value, and price patterns over 25 years, including by fertilizer type.
Requires lists of imported fertilizer types, importing companies (foreign and domestic) with quantities, and source countries.
Requires a description of how anti-dumping and countervailing duties affect retail fertilizer prices.
Requires a study of industry concentration and whether it has caused anticompetitive effects.
Requires a comparison of emerging fertilizers (including biological ones) with conventional ones on price, efficiency, and yield.
Requires an assessment of regulations, including where regulatory burden is hampering production, distribution, and use.
Requires an evaluation of price reporting transparency and a recommendation to Congress on whether to require industry price reporting.
Requires a look at projected market growth and economic and political risks.
Bars the report from including confidential business information.

Fertilizer manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers
USDA and its Economic Research Service
Congress and policymakers who weigh fertilizer rules, trade duties, and competition policy
Consumers and communities indirectly, through food prices and fertilizer's environmental effects

benefits: A public, government-written study could give farmers, buyers, and lawmakers clearer information about how the fertilizer market works.
Reviewing price reporting could show whether market information is open enough for people who buy and sell fertilizer.
Comparing newer products with conventional ones could give farmers information about options such as biological fertilizers.
Recommendations on price reporting frequency could inform future decisions by Congress.
concerns: The report would be a study only, so it may not lead to any direct change in fertilizer prices or competition.
Listing importers and source countries could reveal business relationships, although the bill says confidential business information would be left out.

label: S. 764
title: Colorado Outdoor Recreation and Economy Act
short_title: Colorado Outdoor Recreation and Economy Act
one: The bill would protect large areas of Colorado public land as wilderness, wildlife conservation areas, special management areas, and a new national recreation area. It would also block new oil and gas leasing in the Thompson Divide, pay existing leaseholders who give up their leases with credits, and start a pilot program to capture coal mine methane.
summary: This bill covers four areas of Colorado. In the Continental Divide area, it adds about 30,000 acres to wilderness (Ptarmigan Peak, Holy Cross, Eagles Nest, and the new Hoosier Ridge and Tenmile wilderness areas). It sets aside about 8,000 acres of the Williams Fork Mountains as potential wilderness, with a delay tied to a decision on livestock grazing. It also creates three wildlife conservation areas, including a wildlife corridor over Interstate 70. In the San Juan Mountains, it adds wilderness to Lizard Head, Mount Sneffels, and the new McKenna Peak Wilderness. It creates two special management areas and releases some leftover study lands from further wilderness consideration. In the Thompson Divide, it bars new mineral leasing and mining on federal land. Companies that give up existing oil and gas leases there can get credits, which they can use against bids, royalties, or rent on other federal oil and gas leases in Colorado. It also starts a pilot program to inventory, lease, capture, or destroy methane leaking from coal mines. In the Curecanti area, it creates a roughly 50,300-acre National Park Service recreation area. That area keeps hunting, fishing, boating, and most existing grazing, and it keeps dam and water operations in place. Across the bill, existing grazing and water rights are mostly protected, tribal treaty rights and traditional uses are kept, and military overflights stay allowed. The bill creates no protective buffer zones around the new areas.
does: Adds roughly 30,000 acres to the White River National Forest wilderness system, including the new Hoosier Ridge and Tenmile Wilderness areas.
Designates the Williams Fork Mountains as potential wilderness. It becomes full wilderness after a grazing decision and any range improvements, or after a set period.
Creates the Porcupine Gulch, Williams Fork Mountains, and Spraddle Creek Wildlife Conservation Areas, with limits on motor vehicles, new roads, and commercial logging.
Allows the Interstate 70 and Eisenhower-Johnson Tunnels projects to use the subsurface under the Porcupine Gulch area. It also lets the Secretary make minor boundary changes for highway work.
Adds wilderness to Lizard Head and Mount Sneffels and creates the McKenna Peak Wilderness (BLM land) in the San Juan Mountains.

Creates the Sheep Mountain and Liberty Bell East Special Management Areas, with no permanent roads and limited motor use. Existing permitted activities, such as helicopter access and a running event, may continue.
Releases the rest of the Dominguez Canyon and McKenna Peak Wilderness Study Areas from wilderness study status, so they are no longer protected as study areas.
Withdraws the new protected areas, a 6,590-acre Naturita Canyon area, and the Thompson Divide from new mining claims, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing, subject to valid existing rights.

Lets leaseholders give up Thompson Divide oil and gas leases in exchange for credits. The credits equal bonus bids, rentals paid, and certain permit-preparation expenses. They can be applied to other federal oil and gas payments in Colorado, and the surrendered leases are permanently cancelled.
Sets up a pilot program to inventory coal mine methane leaks, lease or authorize capture or destruction of that methane, cap or destroy what remains, and report to Congress within 4 years.

Establishes the Curecanti National Recreation Area (about 50,300 acres) as a National Park System unit. It transfers some Forest Service, BLM, and Reclamation land to the Park Service, protects water rights, and keeps hunting, fishing, and boating.
Requires the Secretary to fulfill a 26-mile public fishing easement obligation in the Upper Gunnison Basin within 10 years.
Protects tribal treaty rights and traditional ceremonial and plant-gathering uses on the covered lands.
States that military overflights and airspace use are not restricted, and expresses the sense of Congress that military aviation training is critical.
who: Colorado residents and communities near the affected public lands, including Summit, Eagle, Grand, San Miguel, Gunnison, Pitkin, Garfield, and Delta counties
Hikers, hunters, anglers, boaters, skiers, and other outdoor recreation users
Wildlife, including migratory animals that cross Interstate 70, and the plants, forests, and watersheds in the protected areas
Ranchers and livestock grazing permit holders
Oil and gas leaseholders in the Thompson Divide and coal mine lessees in the pilot area
Federal taxpayers, because the credits are applied against payments owed to the government
Federal land agencies (Forest Service, BLM, National Park Service, Bureau of Reclamation)
Indian Tribes with treaty rights or traditional uses on these lands
Downstream water users who rely on these watersheds

benefits: Adding wilderness and conservation areas could help protect land, water, and wildlife habitat in these areas.
A wildlife corridor over Interstate 70 may help animals cross the highway more safely.
Keeping hunting, fishing, and boating in the Curecanti area may protect existing outdoor recreation.
Ending new mineral leasing and mining in Thompson Divide could reduce future development there.
The coal mine methane pilot program could reduce methane leaks, though the material does not state the size of any effect.
concerns: Barring new mining and leasing in Thompson Divide may limit future energy and mineral production there.
Credits for giving up oil and gas leases could be used on other federal leases in Colorado, which may affect how federal energy revenue is collected elsewhere.
Delaying the Williams Fork Mountains decision until a grazing decision is made could leave the land's status uncertain for some time.
Because the bill creates no buffer zones, activities just outside the new areas may still affect them.
Some ranchers or water users may worry that new rules could change how they use land or water, even though existing grazing and water rights are mostly protected.
imp.cost: ["The material provided does not state the cost of this bill or how it would be funded."]
unknowns: The material does not say how the Williams Fork grazing decision will be made or how long the delay could last.
The material does not say how the credit system for relinquished leases will be valued or how much it could affect federal revenue.
The material does not say how much methane the coal mine pilot program could capture or destroy.
The material does not describe how the wildlife corridor over Interstate 70 would be built or paid for.
The material does not say what the 'mostly' protected grazing and water rights exceptions are.
The material does not describe the bill's effect on local economies or tourism.
The bill's current status is listed as in Senate committee (hearing or markup), so its final form may change.

stage.last_action: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining. Hearings held. With printed Hearing: S.Hrg. 119-237.

water.reason: Permanent protection of watersheds in the Continental Divide, San Juan, and Thompson Divide areas, plus a ban on new leasing there, shields headwaters from development, though existing water rights and dam operations are kept as they are.

air.reason: The coal mine methane pilot program requires inventorying, capturing, or destroying leaking methane, which reduces a potent greenhouse gas and air pollutant.

transparency.reason: The bill does not clearly change public access to information or government decision-making processes.

people_over_profit.reason: Withdrawing Thompson Divide minerals from leasing and limiting development in protected areas puts public land and resource values ahead of extraction profits, though existing leases and rights are largely preserved.

local_say.reason: Local communities gain some protected areas and a recreation area, but the bill is a federal designation process and the effects on local decision-making are mixed or unclear.

no_bailouts.reason: Lease surrender credits that can be applied against bids, royalties, and rents on other Colorado federal leases give companies value from federal payments, which functions as a tax-like break paid for by taxpayers.

news.overall: Lean Left coverage in these headlines touches on disaster relief, environmental policy, and recreation economics, but it does not explicitly name the bill. label: H.R. 10117
title: GATOR Act of 2026
one: The bill orders a Government Accountability Office-led study of how the federal "similarity of appearance" protection for American alligators, common caimans and brown caimans has affected their populations and removal of nuisance or invasive animals.
summary: This bill does not change any law or loosen any protection. It only asks for a study. The Comptroller General, who leads the Government Accountability Office (a nonpartisan congressional watchdog), would work with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and wildlife agencies in states that have American alligators, common caimans or brown caimans. The study would look at a federal rule under the Endangered Species Act. Under that rule, some reptiles are treated as "threatened" only because they look like a protected species. This is called "similarity of appearance." The goal is to prevent confusion and illegal trade in protected look-alikes. The study would ask how this treatment has affected the animals' populations and state management programs. It would also ask whether the treatment led to the American alligator recovering more than fully, and whether it led the caiman to become invasive in Florida. Finally, it would ask whether the treatment has made it harder to remove nuisance alligators or invasive caimans from waterways near homes and businesses. The bill sets no deadline, no dollar amount, and no new rules. Any later changes would need separate action by Congress or the agency. The bill's wording assumes some of these effects happened, and the study is meant to test that.

Requires consultation with the Interior Secretary (through Fish and Wildlife Service) and relevant state wildlife agencies.
Examines how the "similarity of appearance" threatened listing affected populations and state management programs.
Asks whether the listing led to more than full recovery of alligators and to caimans becoming invasive in Florida.
Asks whether the listing made removing nuisance alligators or invasive caimans near homes and businesses harder.
Does not change any protections, set a deadline, or give money.

The study could help show whether the rule has helped or hurt alligator and caiman management in states.
Findings could help people near waterways understand whether removing nuisance reptiles is harder under current rules.
concerns: Some people may worry that the study is framed to suggest the rule has caused problems, which could lead to later pressure to weaken it.
Because the study is not set up to be neutral about its findings, critics may question whether it fully tests the bill's assumptions.
The rule exists to reduce confusion and illegal trade in protected look-alikes; weakening it could make enforcement harder.

label: H.R. 10280
title: 9–8–8 Implementation Act of 2026
one: The bill would fund and expand the 9-8-8 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline and related crisis care by paying for call centers, facilities, workforce training, and a media campaign, and by requiring insurers, Medicare, Medicaid and other programs to cover crisis response services.
summary: This bill aims to strengthen the 9-8-8 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline and the care that people get after they call. It would authorize new grants for local and regional crisis call centers, for hiring, training, and technology. It would raise funding for a pilot program that pairs mental health responders with emergency calls. It would also create a national suicide prevention media campaign and authorize $1 billion for building and renovating crisis facilities, such as health centers, crisis stabilization units, and call centers. Workforce programs would be expanded to train more crisis workers, including a fellowship for minority students. The bill would require Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, federal employee health plans, VA reimbursement, and private insurers to cover "crisis response services," with cost-sharing no stricter than for medical and surgical care. Most coverage rules start 3 years after enactment. It would set up a federal panel to recommend training and protocols for 9-1-1 dispatchers, including when to send callers to crisis care instead of police, and to set data standards with privacy protections. It would make Medicaid enhanced funding for mobile crisis and other crisis services permanent, and it would change the Medicaid "IMD exclusion" (a rule that limits Medicaid payment to some large mental health facilities) so that certain crisis facilities and clinics are not covered by it. Most spending is "authorized," meaning Congress must still vote to actually fund it.

one: Creates a new national park unit at Fort Ontario in Oswego, New York, to preserve the story of 982 World War II Holocaust refugees sheltered there in 1944–46, once enough land has been acquired.
summary: This bill would create the Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park in New York as part of the National Park System. Its purpose is to protect and teach about the 982 World War II refugees who were housed at Fort Ontario from August 1944 to February 1946. The park would not officially exist right away. First, the Secretary of the Interior must decide that enough land inside a mapped "Proposed Boundary" has been acquired to make a manageable park. Then, within 30 days, the Secretary must announce the park in the Federal Register, the government's daily public notice publication. The National Park Service could get land by donation, by purchase using donated or appropriated (Congress-approved) money, or by land swap. Land owned by New York State or local governments could only be donated, not bought. The Park Service could sign agreements with the state and with public or private groups to offer education and interpretation, and to restore historic resources on nearby non-federal land. If the Park Service helps with non-federal land, the public must have reasonable access. Within three fiscal years after money is provided, the Park Service must finish a general management plan, working with the state. The bill does not say how much money would be needed. The map is to be available for public inspection.

label: H.R. 10654
title: PFB Act
short_title: PFB Act (Protecting our Forces' Benefits Act)
one: The bill would require the military to give an honorable discharge, and would protect veterans benefit eligibility, to service members separated solely because of pseudofolliculitis barbae, a painful skin condition caused by shaving.
summary:
Pseudofolliculitis barbae (PFB) is a skin condition, often called razor bumps. It happens when shaved hairs curl back into the skin and cause pain and inflammation. It is more common in people with coarse, curly hair, and it affects Black men at especially high rates. Military grooming rules usually require a clean-shaven face, and some service members have been discharged because they could not meet those rules because of PFB.

This bill deals with what happens after such a discharge. It says the military branch's Secretary must label the separation as "honorable" when the only reason for the discharge is PFB. It also says a person separated solely because of PFB cannot be denied Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) benefits just because they did not serve the minimum amount of active duty time normally required by section 5303A of title 38 of the U.S. Code.

The bill does not change grooming rules, does not say whether shaving waivers must be granted, and does not set up a new benefits program. It only fixes the discharge label and waives the minimum-service rule for these cases. The text does not say whether it applies to past discharges or only to future ones, and it does not give a start date. It also does not give a cost estimate.

label: H.R. 177
title: Yosemite National Park Equal Access and Fairness Act
short_title: Yosemite Equal Access and Fairness Act (Hetch Hetchy)
one: Raises the rent San Francisco pays for its Hetch Hetchy dam and reservoir in Yosemite from $30,000 to $2 million a year, bars passing that cost to wholesale customers, and directs the Park Service to open the reservoir and Lake Eleanor areas to recreation such as swimming, boating, and camping.
summary:
In 1913, Congress passed the Raker Act, which let San Francisco dam the Hetch Hetchy Valley inside Yosemite National Park for water and power. San Francisco pays $30,000 a year in rent for this. This bill would raise the rent to $2 million a year and adjust it each year for inflation. San Francisco's utility could not recover that money from the wholesale water or power customers it sells to. The bill also lets the rent money be used for wildfire mitigation (reducing fire risk), as well as other improvements.

The bill also adds a new section telling the National Park Service to manage the Hetch Hetchy Reservoir and Lake Eleanor Basin for public recreation. It says the agency should preserve scenic, historic, and scientific features. Swimming, non-motorized boating, camping above the high-water mark, picnicking, and other approved activities would be allowed. The Secretary of the Interior could set limits and rules. These activities must not conflict with each area's primary use. Vehicles could use the access roads as long as they do not harm dam operations.

Within one year, the Park Service must report to Congress. The report would cover whether the 1913 access intent has been followed. It would also look at how to fund access, including changing water and power prices, treating San Francisco as a concessioner (a business operating in a park), and adding the value of lost recreation and flood control to the rent.

Yosemite National Park Equal Access and Fairness Act
This bill modifies the Raker Act, which allowed San Francisco to dam the Hetch Hetchy Valley within Yosemite National Park, to (1) increase the annual rent San Francisco pays to the National Park Service (NPS), and (2) direct the NPS to expand public access to the reservoir and lake created by the dam.

label: H.R. 3708
title: No Place for LGBTQ+ Hate Act
short_title: No Place for LGBTQ+ Hate Act
one: The bill would cancel five 2025 executive orders on sex and gender identity (covering federal definitions of sex, military service, youth gender-related health care, school sports, and school instruction) and bar federal money from being used to carry them out.
summary:
This bill would wipe out five executive orders (directives from the President) signed in early 2025 that deal with transgender, nonbinary, and intersex people. It says those orders, plus any "related or successor" orders that "similarly harm or limit the rights" of LGBTQI+ people, would have no legal force. It also says no federal money could be used to put them into effect.

The five orders are: EO 14168, which sets the federal government's definition of sex and limits identity markers such as those on IDs; EO 14183, which reinstates and expands a military ban on transgender service members; EO 14187, which directs agencies to act to stop gender-related medical care for people under 19; EO 14201, which bars transgender girls and women from school sports teams matching their gender identity; and EO 14190, which deals with schools and how they address gender identity. The bill's own wording describes these orders in strongly critical terms.

The bill has a savings clause saying it does not reduce any constitutional power of the President. The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee and several others. It would take effect only if passed by both chambers and signed, or if a veto were overridden. Its text does not include a start date or an estimate of cost.

label: H.R. 3717
title: Golden Mussel Eradication and Control Act of 2025
short_title: Golden Mussel Eradication and Control Act of 2025
one: The bill sets up a five-year federal program, led by the Aquatic Nuisance Species Task Force, to research, monitor, control and wipe out the invasive golden mussel, starting in California's Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, with $15 million a year authorized.
summary:
The golden mussel is a small invasive shellfish that has shown up in California's Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta. It can clog water pipes, pumps and fish screens, and it can harm native fish and water quality. This bill would change an existing law on aquatic invasive species to create a demonstration (pilot) program aimed at the golden mussel. The federal Aquatic Nuisance Species Task Force would run it, working with state and local governments, port authorities, industry, universities and local nonprofits.

The program would fund research on the mussel's biology, how it affects fish and water quality, and how well different control tools work. It would build an early warning system to predict where the mussel will spread next. It would also develop plans to remove it from boats, abandoned boats, public works, fish screens and waterways, including boat hull inspections. Within one year, the Task Force would write guidelines for controlling the mussel, which could include boat inspection stations.

The bill also creates a competitive grant program for projects that find better ways to remove mussels from water intakes, pipes, screens, boats and waterways. The Task Force could make agreements for the use or sale of new technology developed under the grants. It could hand parts of the work to other agencies if that would work better. Congress would authorize $15 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. Authorizing money does not guarantee it is spent. A separate spending bill would still be needed.

one: The bill would require the VA to extend its written informed-consent rules for long-term opioid pain therapy to also cover antipsychotics, stimulants, antidepressants, anxiety medications, and narcotics.
summary: This bill would change how the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) handles certain prescriptions. Right now, a VA Health Administration rule called Directive 1005 (dated May 13, 2020) sets out how doctors must get a patient's informed consent before starting long-term opioid treatment for pain. The bill orders the VA Secretary to update that directive so the same kind of consent process applies to five more types of drugs: antipsychotics, stimulants, antidepressants, anti-anxiety medicines (anxiolytics), and narcotics. It also does not spell out which specific drugs count within each category. The bill has been referred to a House subcommittee and has not advanced further.

label: H.R. 4987
title: Food Date Labeling Act of 2025
one: Sets one national standard for the wording of voluntary "best by" and "use by" dates on food labels, and blocks states and localities from requiring different wording.
summary: Today, food makers use many different phrases for dates on packages, such as "sell by," "best before," "use by," and "expires on." Shoppers often don't know which ones mean the food is unsafe and which only mean the quality may slip. This bill would create two standard phrases. If a company chooses to print a quality date, it must put "BEST If Used By" in front of it. If it chooses to print a date after which the food should be thrown away, it must use "USE By." Short forms, "BB" and "UB," are allowed only when the package is too small. Companies may add "or freeze by." Dates must be easy to read and easy to find. Putting a date on a package stays optional. The bill covers foods overseen by the FDA and the USDA (meat, poultry, and eggs), but not infant formula. Within two years, the agencies must write rules and start a consumer education campaign. The rules would apply to foods labeled two years after the bill becomes law. The agencies could later pick different standard phrases. Labels that break the rules would count as "misbranded" under federal food laws. The bill also overrides state and local rules about date wording. It bars states and cities from banning the sale or donation of food after its quality date. States may still ban sales or donations after a discard date. People's ability to sue under existing state or federal law is preserved.

crs:
Food Date Labeling Act of 2025
This bill establishes uniform requirements for quality and discard date phrases (e.g., 
best by
 and 
use by
) placed voluntarily on food labels.
Specifically, if a food is labeled with a quality date (i.e., the date after which the quality of the item may deteriorate), the label must include the phrase 
BEST If Used By
 or the abbreviation 
BB
. Similarly, if a food is labeled with a discard date (i.e., the date after which the item should not be consumed), the label must include the phrase 
USE By
 or the abbreviation 
UB
. Abbreviations may be used only if an item’s packaging is too small to fit the full phrase.
Quality and discard dates must be written in a single, easy-to-read font and placed in a prominent location on an item’s label or package. The phrase 
or freeze by
 may be added after a quality or discard date phrase where appropriate.
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Department of Agriculture (USDA) must promulgate regulations to carry out these provisions and ensure that the uniform phrases are standardized across all food products. HHS and USDA may specify alternative quality and discard date phrases through regulations.
The bill specifies that no state or local government may enforce a requirement related to quality and discard date phrases that differs from the requirements of the bill. The bill does not apply to infant formula, which is subject to separate labeling requirements under current law.

label: H.R. 5935
title: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians Water Rights Settlement Act
short_title: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians Water Rights Settlement Act
one: Ratifies a settlement of long-running water lawsuits between the Agua Caliente Band, two Coachella Valley water agencies, and the U.S., confirming a 20,000 acre-feet-per-year groundwater right, spending $500 million in federal money, and moving about 2,700 acres of federal land into trust for the Tribe.
summary:
This bill would approve a deal, signed May 19, 2025, that ends water lawsuits between the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians and two local water agencies, the Coachella Valley Water District (CVWD) and the Desert Water Agency (DWA). The Tribe's right to pump up to 20,000 acre-feet of groundwater a year from the Indio Subbasin (the aquifer under the Palm Springs area) would be confirmed. That right dates to 1876–77 and would take priority over the agencies' claims to native groundwater. The Tribe would also keep its rights to certain creeks.

The federal government would put $500 million into a trust fund for the Tribe: $300 million for water projects, $100 million to reimburse the water agencies for groundwater-recharge projects, $50 million for water management, and $50 million for operations and upkeep. Amounts would be adjusted for construction cost inflation. In exchange, the Tribe and the U.S. would give up many past and some future water claims. They keep claims under the Clean Water Act, the Safe Drinking Water Act and the Superfund law (CERCLA), and claims over misconduct.

The bill moves about 2,700 acres of Bureau of Land Management land into trust for the Tribe, bars gaming on it, and lets CVWD buy about 842 acres at fair market value. It sets up a Tribal possessory-interest tax that replaces the county property tax on those interests, with payments to other local agencies. It also adds protections for Native cultural resources. It takes effect only after several conditions are met, and expires if they aren't met by the end of 2035.

who: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians and its members and allottees (individual trust landholders)

U.S. taxpayers who fund the $500 million
Users of the Indio Subbasin aquifer in the Palm Springs/Coachella Valley area

benefits: Could end more than a decade of costly litigation (cases filed 2013 and 2020) and give all parties certainty about groundwater use.
Funds recycling, infrastructure, and groundwater-recharge projects that may improve water supply and reliability in a drought-prone aquifer.

Keeps Tribal, federal, and citizen-style water quality claims under the Clean Water Act, Safe Drinking Water Act and Superfund, and requires the Interior Secretary to follow NEPA and the Endangered Species Act for projects.
Honors a senior Tribal water right and adds cultural resource and burial protections at the CVWD facility; bars gaming on transferred land.
Allottees get a tribal process with appeals, then federal recourse; the tax deal requires the Tribe to pay other local agencies at least what they would have received, enforceable in federal court.
Public notice: the Secretary must publish findings in the Federal Register before the deal takes effect, and the Tribe must file annual expenditure reports.
concerns: Costs U.S. taxpayers $500 million in mandatory spending, with automatic inflation adjustments that could raise the total.
Waives many damage claims, including past overdraft, subsidence, and water-quality claims where water meets standards; some of these releases are broad and cover unknown claims.
The Tribal water right is not subject to state law or the replenishment charge, and can't be lost through non-use. This could shift aquifer management costs to other pumpers or ratepayers.
The $100 million to reimburse water agencies could be seen as taxpayer money subsidizing local utilities.
Executing the Agreement is declared not a major federal action under NEPA, which limits environmental review of that step; the Tribe prepares environmental documents for later projects.
Land transfers override protections tied to the Santa Rosa and San Jacinto Mountains National Monument and the California Desert Protection Act, and withdraw the land from mining and other uses.
The Tribal tax preempts county property tax, which could reduce local government oversight; the Tribe need not pay other agencies more than they'd otherwise get.
Off-reservation leasing of water for up to 99 years, with Secretary approval, could affect neighboring communities.
Some expenditure details and tribal rate-setting for reservation customers are in the Agreement, which I could not see.

label: H.R. 6182
title: Find It Early Act
one: Requires private insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE and VA care to cover extra breast cancer imaging (like ultrasound and MRI) with no out-of-pocket costs for people at higher risk or with dense breasts, and for others whose doctor says they need it.
summary:
This bill would make breast cancer screening and follow-up imaging free to patients in more cases. Today, a standard mammogram is often covered at no cost, but extra tests, like ultrasounds, MRIs, or other advanced imaging, can leave patients with big bills. Under this bill, people at higher risk of breast cancer, or with dense breast tissue, could get these tests with no copays, deductibles, or coinsurance. Higher risk would be judged using guidelines from the American College of Radiology and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network. People not in those groups would also get free imaging if their health care provider decides they need it, based on things like age, race, ethnicity, or personal or family medical history. The tests would be covered as often as the cancer network's guidelines recommend.

The rule would apply to job-based and individual health plans, including older "grandfathered" plans. It would also apply to Medicare (including Medicare Advantage), Medicaid, military TRICARE coverage, and Veterans Affairs care. Veterans would qualify even if they are not enrolled in VA health care. Most parts would start January 1, 2026, a date that has already passed or is close, since the bill was introduced in November 2025. States could get extra time for Medicaid if they need to pass new state laws. The bill text does not include a cost estimate or funding plan.

label: H.R. 6806
title: Antisemitism Response and Prevention Act of 2025
short_title: Antisemitism Response and Prevention Act of 2025
one: Creates a permanent, nonpartisan DOJ office to coordinate efforts against antisemitism, builds a new FBI hate crime reporting center, adds campus civil rights duties, protects the Education Dept. civil rights office, and bars political conditions on nonprofit security grants.
summary:
This bill is aimed at fighting antisemitism (hostility toward Jewish people) while also limiting what its authors call political misuse of that fight. It would set up a Justice Department office, led by a non-political career official with a four-year term, to coordinate federal work against antisemitism using the 2023 national strategy. It would also create an FBI Hate Crime Reporting Center to collect and publish data on hate crimes against all groups, and run a public awareness campaign.

Colleges that take federal student aid would have to name a staff member to handle Title VI (federal anti-discrimination law) complaints, run an awareness campaign, publish yearly reports, and tell apart illegal discrimination from protected political speech. The bill would authorize $280 million a year for the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights, require it to reopen regional offices closed since January 2025, and bar moving or closing it without new law. It would raise the Nonprofit Security Grant Program to $500 million a year and bar conditions tied to diversity programs, immigration, or political views. It also requires reports on extremism in prisons and law enforcement and on domestic terrorism. The findings and a "sense of Congress" section sharply criticize the current administration's antisemitism policies and say the IHRA definition shouldn't be used in deportation or criminal cases. These sections are statements of opinion and carry no legal force.

one: The bill expands a Department of Homeland Security school safety information center to offer training, research on wearable panic alarms, a national school safety data hub, and standards for school emergency maps that federal money can buy.
summary: This bill would build up the Federal Clearinghouse on School Safety Evidence-based Practices, which sits inside the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). It would have DHS run public education on preventing and responding to school emergencies, including school shootings. It would also have DHS give training and one-on-one consulting to schools and states, and hire experts. DHS would run a program to develop and test wearable "panic alarm" devices that connect to emergency services. It would also set up a National School Safety Data Center on SchoolSafety.gov within one year. The center would collect and publish data on school violence, injuries, deaths, safety plans, and other issues such as fights and truancy. A Director of the Clearinghouse would be named within 120 days, and the Secret Service would be brought into the process. The bill also bars any federal money from buying emergency response maps of school buildings unless they meet technical rules, including that the school owns the data, it is stored in the U.S., and it is checked every year by a walk-through. DHS must send Congress a strategy within a year and yearly reports on its work. A later report on "master plans" for school shooting prevention would be due in four years. The bill says it gives the Clearinghouse no power to make rules. It does not set a dollar amount.

title: To amend the Aamodt Litigation Settlement Act to modify a provision relating to the extension of certain dates for the completion of the Regional Water System, and for other purposes.
short_title: Aamodt Settlement Water System Deadline Extension Bill
one: The bill lets the parties to the Aamodt water settlement in northern New Mexico agree to push back the deadlines for finishing the Regional Water System if they all agree an extension is reasonably necessary.
summary:
This bill changes a 2010 law, the Aamodt Litigation Settlement Act. That law ended a decades-long court fight over water rights in the Pojoaque Basin near Santa Fe, New Mexico. Part of the deal was building a Regional Water System. The system would deliver clean water to four Pueblos (Nambé, Pojoaque, San Ildefonso and Tesuque) and to nearby non-Pueblo residents. The 2010 law sets dates by which the system must be substantially finished. If those dates are missed, parts of the settlement could expire or fall apart.

H.R. 6869 would add a new paragraph to the section about those deadlines. It says the dates in subsection (e) may be extended if five parties all agree an extension is reasonably necessary. Those parties are the Pueblos, the United States (through the Secretary of the Interior), the State of New Mexico, the City of Santa Fe, and Santa Fe County. The bill also relabels the existing text in that section. It does not add money, and it does not say how long an extension could last. The bill text does not say what the current deadlines are or how the section would work in detail. I could only see the bill's short amendment, not the full underlying law, and no Congressional Research Service summary is available yet.

It would go inside Manassas National Battlefield Park in Virginia. The Secretary of the Interior would pick the groups or people who build each memorial. The Secretary would also approve the location, size, design, and inscriptions. If fundraisers falsely claim ties to the memorials or the federal government, the Secretary could suspend their authority. label: H.R. 7976
title: Moral Injury Recognition and Restitution Act
short_title: Moral Injury Recognition and Restitution Act
one: Requires the VA to backdate disability compensation for veterans whose approved claims are based on military sexual trauma to the day after they left military service, with back pay.
summary: Today, when a veteran gets approved for VA disability pay, the start date usually depends on when the claim was filed or other timing rules. That means many veterans who waited years to speak up about sexual assault or harassment during service only get paid from a later date. This bill would change that for one group: veterans whose claims are approved because of military sexual trauma (MST). For these veterans, the VA would have to treat the start date of the benefit as the day after they were discharged. The VA would then pay the money owed from that date forward, as a lump of back pay. The bill covers mental health conditions tied to MST, using a definition already in federal law, and also any physical injury or disease caused or made worse by MST. It does not change how a claim is decided. A veteran still has to be approved first. The bill does not say how much it would cost or when it would start, and no official cost estimate or CRS summary is available yet. The bill was sent to the House Veterans' Affairs Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee.

label: H.R. 8276
title: Quindaro Townsite National Historic Landmark Act
short_title: Quindaro Townsite National Historic Landmark Act
one: Designates the Quindaro Townsite in Kansas City, Kansas, a Free-State and Underground Railroad site, as a National Historic Landmark and lets the Interior Secretary partner with and fund local groups to protect and interpret it, without limiting what property owners can do.
summary:
This bill would officially name the Quindaro Townsite in Kansas City, Kansas, a National Historic Landmark. Quindaro was founded in 1857 to help the Free-State side in the fight over whether Kansas would allow slavery. It served as a Missouri River port for people opposed to slavery and as a stop on the Underground Railroad, where people escaping slavery could reach freedom. Archaeologists have found many artifacts there, and more may be found.

After the designation, the Secretary of the Interior could sign cooperative agreements with public or private groups. These agreements would aim to protect historic resources at the site and provide education and interpretation programs for the public. The Secretary would talk with the State of Kansas, Kansas City, Kansas, and nearby local governments first. The Secretary could also give technical and financial help to those partners. The bill does not say how much money, and it does not set a budget.

The bill says the designation would not stop property owners, including owners of the landmark, from doing what they could otherwise do with their property. It also says that Kansas City, Kansas, and the State would keep running the site as they do now. In other words, there is no federal takeover and no new federal land ownership in the text. The bill was introduced by a Republican with a Democratic cosponsor from Missouri and one from Kansas, and had a subcommittee hearing in September 2026.

label: H.R. 8546
title: Pechanga Band of Indians Water Rights Settlement Technical Amendments Act
short_title: Pechanga Water Rights Settlement Technical Amendments Act
one: Makes technical fixes to a 2016 water rights settlement with the Pechanga Band in Southern California: it clarifies what land counts as the reservation and lets a water quality fund pay for more than just desalination.
summary: In 2016, Congress approved a settlement of water rights claims involving the Pechanga Band of Luiseño Mission Indians in Southern California. This bill makes small fixes to that law. First, it rewrites the definition of the Band's "Reservation" so it lists the specific 1882 and 1907 executive orders and the dates when land was later added (from 1893 through 2008). It also says the Reservation includes land next to it that the U.S. holds in trust for the Band on the settlement's enforceability date. It also includes nearby land placed in trust later, if that land lies inside the Santa Margarita River Watershed. Second, it changes how the Pechanga Water Quality Account can be used. Today the money is tied to groundwater desalination in the Wolf Valley Basin. The bill would let it pay for any activities that address water quality problems in that basin. Third, it tells the Secretary of the Interior to promptly sign matching changes to the settlement agreement, which Congress says the parties already agreed to. The bill says it does not change the settlement's legal start conditions, the Secretary's 2020 finding that those conditions were met, or any existing water right. The text does not give a cost estimate, and no CRS summary was available.

one: The bill would transfer about 21,578 acres of federal land in the Denali National Park and Preserve to the Alaska Native corporation Doyon, Limited, ban mining and sale of that land, and shrink the preserve's boundary.
summary:
This bill would make the Secretary of the Interior give about 21,578 acres of federal land inside the preserve part of Denali National Park and Preserve to Doyon, Limited. Doyon is an Alaska Native regional corporation. The land is what Doyon chose in 1978 under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA), a 1971 law that settled Alaska Native land claims. The transfer must happen within one year of the bill becoming law. It is subject to valid existing rights, and the government must keep the public access easements that ANCSA requires. The land includes the Geese House, a site with cultural importance. The bill says Doyon could not sell or transfer the land to anyone except the United States. The bill says the transfer would not have to follow the usual federal conveyance regulations or any past land withdrawals (earlier federal protections). It would also redraw the park boundary to leave out the transferred land. The bill text does not explain why this site is being transferred or how the Geese House is used. It has no cost estimate, and no CRS summary is available yet.

label: H.R. 9017

one: The bill would declare that a 2020 U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service wildlife-protection review already satisfies the Endangered Species Act for the EPA's approval of Florida taking over federal wetland dredge-and-fill permitting, and would bar any further wildlife consultation on it.
summary:
Under the Clean Water Act, anyone who wants to dredge or fill wetlands and certain waters needs a "Section 404" permit, which is normally issued by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. A state can ask the EPA for permission to run that program itself. In December 2020, the EPA approved Florida's request. Before that approval, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service wrote a "biological opinion," which is an expert review of how the action could harm endangered species. It included an "incidental take statement," which says how much harm to protected species is allowed.

This bill would say two things by law. First, that the 2020 biological opinion meets the requirements of the Endangered Species Act, and that following it counts as following the Act, for the EPA's approval of Florida's program. Second, that no more consultation with wildlife agencies is needed under section 7(a) of the Act. The bill also says the "Agency Action" covers "other activities," a phrase it defines only by pointing to the glossary of the biological opinion. That glossary was not provided, so the full reach is unclear. The bill does not change the text of the Endangered Species Act or the Clean Water Act. It does limit how the Act applies to this one approval. The bill text does not say why it is needed. It does not mention any court case or other background.

label: H.R. 9221
title: Outdoor Americans with Disabilities Act
one: The bill would make it much harder for the Forest Service and Interior Department to close roads on federal public land, using disability access as the stated reason, and would speed up road changes by skipping some environmental review.
summary:
This bill covers National Forest land and land managed by the Interior Department, such as Bureau of Land Management land. It tells the agencies to make updating their travel and motor vehicle use plans a priority. It also sets rules for deciding which roads stay open to cars, off-road vehicles, e-bikes, and snow vehicles.

Any square mile of public land that has at least 2.5 miles of authorized motor-vehicle road is called "disability-accessible land." On that land, agencies could not close roads if the closure would drop the land below that threshold. There are narrow exceptions: a temporary or emergency road less than a year old, or a road that is a direct safety threat.

On other public land, agencies would have to consider reopening roads closed in the last 10 years. They could not close more roads except for a direct safety threat. They could never close roads they find useful for wildfire work, fuel reduction, or search and rescue.

Any closure would need public notice and a hearing, though these can come after the closure in an emergency. Each closure would require a new road to be built within a year. Closures and new roads would skip full National Environmental Policy Act review (the law that requires environmental studies) unless extraordinary circumstances exist. Roads would be presumed open unless "clear and compelling evidence" shows a closure is needed. Roads with unresolved old right-of-way claims (called RS 2477 claims) would stay open until those claims are settled. The bill does not create new roads in wilderness areas, inventoried roadless areas, primitive areas, or most national parks.

label: H.R. 9590
title: SAFE for Manatees Act
one: Directs the Interior Department (through the Fish and Wildlife Service) to study where manatees could find new warm-water habitat, natural or man-made, as Florida power plants and similar industrial sites that warm the water are shut down, and to publish a report within 180 days.
summary:
Many Florida manatees spend cold winters in warm water that flows out of coastal industrial sites, such as power plants. Some of these sites are being shut down, which will make the water cooler. Manatees can get sick or die from cold stress, so losing these warm spots is a concern.

This bill does not build anything. It tells the Secretary of the Interior, working through the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, to study the problem. The study must find and assess places that could work as habitat. These include natural warm-water spots manatees do not use now, and places where people could build artificial warm-water refuges. The Secretary must also work with the Army Corps of Engineers to develop possible ways to build such refuges, along with construction plans. The Secretary must coordinate with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission.

Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, the Secretary must make a report on the results public. The bill only covers the species Trichechus manatus (the West Indian manatee). It does not give money for construction and does not say how much the study would cost. Any building would need separate approval and funding later.

label: H.R. 10828
title: Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act
short_title: Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act
one: The bill would cancel U.S. permissions that let Russian oil and diesel be sold, require sanctions on Russian oil and gas companies, bar U.S. development-bank deals tied to Russian-owned energy, and require regular reports to Congress.
summary: This bill is aimed at cutting the money Russia earns from oil and gas while its war in Ukraine continues. First, it stops the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC, a government agency that backs overseas investments) from supporting or joining any deal involving energy owned by a Russian foreign person, even if the assets are outside Russia. Second, it cancels five Treasury "general licenses" (blanket permissions) that allowed certain Russian crude oil, petroleum products, and diesel to be delivered and sold, including to India. It also bars the Treasury Secretary from issuing new permissions of this kind for Russian oil, fuel, or natural gas. This ban lasts three years. Third, it expands Congress's power to review sanctions-related actions on Russia, including any licensing actions that help Russian energy sales, until the State Department certifies that Russia has ended its war and committed to a just peace that includes paying Ukraine for war damages. Fourth, within 30 days it calls for sanctions on any Russian person involved in oil and gas extraction, refining, production, or shipping. These include freezing U.S.-linked assets and denying or revoking visas. There are exceptions for humanitarian aid, food, medicine, U.N. obligations, and U.S. intelligence or law enforcement work. Finally, it requires reports to Congress on how the licenses affected Russian oil sales and revenue, and on whether Russian energy companies took part in abducting or deporting Ukrainian civilians, including children.
does: Bars the DFC from supporting or joining any deal involving energy owned by a Russian foreign person, even outside Russia, with criminal and civil penalties borrowed from the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
Makes OFAC General Licenses 133, 134A, 134B, 134C, and 135 (permitting certain Russian oil and diesel sales) have no effect starting on the day the bill becomes law.

Bars Treasury from issuing new general licenses or other authorizations for buying, selling, delivering, or offloading Russian crude oil, petroleum products, diesel, or natural gas; this expires after 3 years.

Expands congressional review under the CAATSA sanctions law to cover executive orders under the Russia national emergency (EO 14024) and licensing actions that help Russian energy sales, until the State Department certifies Russia has ended its war and committed to a just peace including compensation to Ukraine.

Within 30 days, directs the President to impose sanctions on Russian persons involved in oil and gas extraction, refining or production, or maritime transport of oil and gas. These include blocking property in U.S. jurisdiction and denying or revoking visas.

Exempts food, agricultural goods, medicine, medical devices, humanitarian assistance, U.N. headquarters obligations, and authorized U.S. intelligence, law enforcement, and national security activities.

Lets courts see classified evidence behind sanctions decisions privately (ex parte and in camera, meaning without the sanctioned party seeing it), and says this does not create a right to judicial review.
Requires reports to Congress within 30 days and every 60 days for 3 years on the effects of the licenses, including Russian export volumes, prices, government revenue, and production.

Requires reports within 30 days and every 180 days for 2 years on Russian state-owned or state-affiliated energy companies' role in abducting, deporting, or indoctrinating Ukrainian civilians, including children.

one: Requires the VA Secretary to report to Congress on the Warrior Training Advancement Course, which trains transitioning service members for Veterans Benefits Administration jobs, including participation, cost savings, and hiring results.
summary: This bill does not create a new program or change who can get benefits. It asks the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to report on an existing training program called the Warrior Training Advancement Course (WARTAC). WARTAC trains service members who are leaving the military, through the military's Transition Assistance Program (TAP), so they can qualify for certain jobs in the Veterans Benefits Administration. label: H.R. 10966
title: Supporting Veteran Mothers Act of 2026
one: The bill would require VA medical facilities to staff enough dedicated maternity care coordinators for pregnant and postpartum veterans, check staffing every two years, fix shortfalls with action plans, and report publicly on the results.
summary: This bill is about veterans who are pregnant or have recently had a baby and get care through the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA). Maternity care coordinators are VA staff who help line up that care, from the time a pregnancy is confirmed through the postpartum period (the months after birth). The bill would require larger VA medical facilities to have enough of these coordinators. Each coordinator counted would have to work only on maternity coordination, not on unrelated tasks. Every two years, each facility would have to count its coordinators and its pregnant and postpartum patients and check whether it meets the minimum. If it falls short, the facility head would have 45 days to send a plan to the VA Secretary and Congress explaining how and when it will fix the gap, and then carry out the plan. The Secretary could grant a waiver in extraordinary cases, such as a local worker shortage. The VA would write guidance within 180 days of enactment, and the first reviews would be due about 240 days after that. The VA would report to Congress each year for five years and post a public summary online. The bill text does not say how much money it would cost or provide new funding. The staffing ratio wording is also unclear, because it lists two overlapping ratios.

title: No Veteran Left Behind: Housing Retention Act of 2026
short_title: No Veteran Left Behind: Housing Retention Act of 2026
one: The bill would create a VA grant program that pays nonprofits, co-ops, and certain government/tribal entities to provide support services (health, food, transportation, eviction prevention) to lower-income veterans so they can stay in permanent housing and avoid homelessness.
summary:
This bill would add a new section to federal veterans' law. It tells the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to give grants to approved groups that help certain veterans keep their homes. The money would go to private nonprofits, consumer cooperatives (member-owned housing groups), and state, local, or tribal housing agencies. The groups would use it for things like mental health and substance use counseling, food assistance, rides to appointments and job interviews, help with medications, money management, eviction prevention, home accessibility changes, and help finding health care.

To qualify, a veteran must have income at or below 80 percent of the area median (not counting VA disability or pension pay). The veteran must live in permanent housing or be moving into it. The veteran must also be formerly homeless or at risk of homelessness. In addition, the veteran must be 55 or older, terminally or chronically ill, have a chronic substance use disorder, or have a significant medical need.

The VA would favor groups serving veterans leaving homelessness or at risk of returning to it. It must try to spread money fairly across regions, including rural areas and tribal lands. Grantees must tell veterans the VA is paying for services, report each year on what they did, and join case conferences with VA, health providers, and housing providers, following privacy laws. The bill does not state a dollar amount.

label: H.R. 10972
title: NEW HORIZON Act
short_title: NEW HORIZON Act (Orbital Data Center Pilot Program)
one: Requires the Defense Department, through the Defense Innovation Unit, to run a pilot program of up to five years testing commercial orbital data centers and space-based cloud computing for military and intelligence uses.
summary:
This bill would make the Secretary of Defense, working through the Defense Innovation Unit, start a pilot program within one year of the bill becoming law. The pilot would test whether commercially built "orbital data centers" (computers, storage, and networking placed in space) and space-based cloud computing can help with national security missions. These could include intelligence, tracking objects in space, command and control, and moving data. The idea is that processing data in orbit could cut delays and make systems harder to knock out than relying only on ground facilities.

The bill tells the Pentagon to encourage competition from newer, non-traditional defense companies and commercial space firms. It requires strong cybersecurity and supply-chain protections for any service handling sensitive or classified information, including protections against foreign ownership or influence. It also asks the Pentagon to study how to defend these assets from attacks. The Pentagon must consult with the Space Force, the National Reconnaissance Office, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, and others. A briefing to Congress's defense committees is due by December 31, 2028. The authority ends five years after enactment. The bill does not set a dollar amount, and it does not mention environmental review, public reporting, or rules for debris and launches.

Requires consultation with Space Force, military departments, the NRO, the NGA, and space policy officials.
Requires a briefing to congressional defense committees by December 31, 2028, covering results, risks, and recommendations.
Ends the pilot authority five years after enactment.

one: Renames the VA outpatient clinic at 311 Spring Green Boulevard in Victoria, Texas, as the "Master Sergeant Roy P. Benavidez VA Clinic" in honor of a Medal of Honor recipient.

This bill is a naming bill. It would rename the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) community-based outpatient clinic in Victoria, Texas, as the "Master Sergeant Roy P. Benavidez VA Clinic." The clinic is at 311 Spring Green Boulevard. Once the bill becomes law, any federal law, rule, map, or record that mentions the clinic would be read as referring to the new name.
